purpose: Seven parallel web scouts probed the P2 scope for blind spots before the research program was designed. Every gap below fed the 2026-07-30 grilling session; the locked decisions are in PLAN.md. Era teams should treat gap evidence (with URLs) as seed sources.

scouts.lens: Media historian — comparing the 7-era map and 8-field schema against canonical histories of American advertising (Pope, Marchand, Fox, industry data series)

gaps.title: Classified advertising is entirely absent, and it is the money Google actually took first
gaps.claim: The plan never mentions classified advertising, yet classifieds were roughly 40% of newspaper ad revenue at their 2000 peak ($19.6B) and are the canonical pre-digital form of intent-based advertising; the 'what did Google capture' answer is wrong without them.
gaps.why_it_matters: The centerpiece question is what Google changed that let it capture so much ad money. Standard media-economics histories answer: search ads are classifieds' descendant — self-serve, intent-matched, priced per unit, bought by individuals and small businesses, not brands via agencies. Classifieds collapsed 77% between 2000 and 2012 (to $4.6B) as Craigslist, Monster, Cars.com and then Google local/search absorbed the intent money. A history built only on brand display (agencies, spots, CPMs) will misattribute Google's revenue source and miss an entire buyer class (individuals and SMBs) that existed in every era since the 1840s.
gaps.evidence: AEI Carpe Diem, 'Creative Destruction: Newspaper Ad Revenue' (https://www.aei.org/carpe-diem/creative-destruction-newspaper-ad-revenue-continued-its-precipitous-free-fall-in-2014-and-its-likely-to-continue/) — classifieds peaked at $19.6B in 2000, ~40% of newspaper ad revenue, $4.6B by 2012. MinnPost, 'How Craigslist killed the newspapers' golden goose' (http://www.minnpost.com/business/2014/02/how-craigslist-killed-newspapers-golden-goose/). Statista, US newspaper classified revenue since 2000 (https://www.statista.com/statistics/196470/classified-advertising-revenue-of-us-newspapers-since-2000/).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: track classified as a distinct category in every era's SCALE split (it existed from the penny press onward), give it its own PRICING entry (per-line rate card, self-serve), and make its collapse an explicit named thread in eras 5-7 feeding the Google-capture argument.

gaps.title: The schema has no brand vs direct-response vs local money distinction
gaps.claim: The 8-field schema treats 'advertising spend' as one kind of money, but the industry's own data (the Coen series) and all histories split national brand money from local/retail money and from direct-response money — pools that behave completely differently and migrated to Google at different times.
gaps.why_it_matters: Google's first decade captured direct-response and local money (classifieds, Yellow Pages, direct mail budgets, SMB spend); TV brand money held out for another decade and partly still does. If every era's SCALE is a single total, the signature chart will show 'internet grows, print dies' without revealing WHICH money moved — which is the actual answer to the project's central question. This distinction also sets up P3 correctly: ads solved zero-price search because search monetizes intent (DR money), which says something specific about whether ads can fund AI inference.
gaps.evidence: purple motes, 'U.S. advertising expenditure data' (https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/) — the Coen/McCann-Erickson series is natively split national vs local and by medium. NBER WP 28161, 'Aggregate Advertising Expenditure in the US Economy' (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf) — documents category definitions and behavior differences across the series.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure: add a money-type split (national brand / local retail / classified / direct response) as a required sub-dimension of SCALE and BUYERS in every era, so the century chart can be read by money type as well as by medium.

gaps.title: Yellow Pages / directory advertising is missing — the direct ancestor of paid search
gaps.claim: Directory advertising peaked around $14-15B in the US (circa 2005) — comparable to the entire US internet ad market that year — and is never mentioned, despite being the closest structural precursor to AdWords: businesses paying for placement against category-level intent.
gaps.why_it_matters: A media historian would treat Yellow Pages as load-bearing for era 6: Google's local and SMB revenue is substantially ex-directory money, and the Yellow Pages sales force (per-category, tiered placement, annual contracts) is the pricing regime the auction replaced. Its fall from ~$14.7B to ~$1B is one of the cleanest before/after demonstrations of the plan's own thesis, and it is invisible in a brand-display-only history.
gaps.evidence: Vendasta, 'Yellow Pages evolution' and UENI, 'Yellow pages are dead' (https://www.vendasta.com/blog/yellow-pages-evolution/, https://ueni.com/blog/yellow-pages-are-dead/) — peak ~$14.7B in 2005, ~$1.1B by 2024. Local Search Association (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Search_Association) — industry trade history. Coen dataset includes Yellow Pages as a tracked category (purple motes, https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: Yellow Pages as a tracked medium in the century dataset (Coen carries it), plus a short structural comparison in era 6 (directory placement vs auction placement) — it strengthens the centerpiece rather than diluting it.

gaps.title: Direct mail is mis-slotted in era 4 and underweighted everywhere else
gaps.claim: The plan treats direct mail as a 1976-1993 'Segmentation' phenomenon, but mail order dates to Montgomery Ward (1872) and Sears (1888), the Coen series tracks direct mail from 1919 with data from the Direct Mail Advertising Association, and it ran at roughly 12-15%+ of all US ad spend for most of the century — often the #2 or #3 medium, and the largest single category by the mid-2000s.
gaps.why_it_matters: Direct mail is the century-long home of the accountability tradition — keyed coupons, tested copy, measured response (Claude Hopkins' 'Scientific Advertising,' 1923) — which is the intellectual lineage Google's measurable click completed. Placing it in era 4 makes performance marketing look like a 1980s invention and breaks the plan's own signature chart, where direct mail will be a huge visible band from 1919 onward that the prose never explains.
gaps.evidence: USPS OIG, 'Advertising Mail: Past and Present' RARC-WP-16-006 (https://www.uspsoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2023-01/RARC-WP-16-006_0.pdf) — direct mail at 12% of a $184B ad market in 1995 and >40% of direct-marketing media. galbithink.org, 'Annual U.S. Advertising Expenditure Since 1919' (https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm) — direct mail is a core series category from 1919. History and Technology, ''The solid gold mailbox': direct mail... in the postwar United States' (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2373518X.2015.1012863).
gaps.recommendation: Restructure: track direct mail as a category from era 1 onward; move the direct-response/testing tradition thread to eras 1-2 (mail order, Hopkins) and let era 4 cover its database-marketing upgrade, not its birth.

gaps.title: The ad-subsidized zero-price content model predates the plan — penny press 1833, ten-cent magazine 1893
gaps.claim: The structural invention the whole project turns on — content sold below cost, with advertising making up the difference — happened in 1833 (Benjamin Day's New York Sun, explicitly founded as 'an advantageous medium for advertisements') and was industrialized in 1893 (Frank Munsey cutting Munsey's Magazine to 10 cents, below production cost); the plan's era 1 (starting 1840s, focused on agencies/commissions/patent medicines) never names this model.
gaps.why_it_matters: Google's zero-price search funded by ads is a rerun of this exact model, and P3's question (why isn't advertising funding AI inference) is a question about when this model works. Standard histories (Pope, 'The Making of Modern Advertising'; the magazine-revolution literature) treat 1893 as the birth of ad-funded national media. Without it, era 1 reads as an industry-plumbing story and the plan's through-line — attention sold to advertisers subsidizes free content — appears from nowhere in 1994. The 1840s start date also silently excludes the penny press.
gaps.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Penny press' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_press) and American Antiquarian Society, 'The Sun' exhibit (https://collections.americanantiquarian.org/earlyamericannewsmedia/exhibits/show/news-in-antebellum-america/item/71) — the Sun's founding statement and below-cost, ad-funded model. Encyclopedia.com, 'Mass Market Magazine Revolution' and 'Munsey's Magazine' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/media/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/mass-market-magazine-revolution) — 1893 price cut, circulation 250k to 750k, advertising covering below-cost sales.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure era 1: either extend its start to 1833 or open it with the penny press as prologue, and make 'audience subsidized by advertisers' an explicitly named model whose reappearances (radio, broadcast TV, portals, Google) the reader can count.

gaps.title: The agency industry's own 180-year structural arc stops at the 15% commission
gaps.claim: The plan covers agency formation and the 15% commission in era 1 and then drops the agency story; canonical histories treat the later arc as load-bearing — open contract (Ayer, 1875), agencies producing radio/TV programs, death of the commission (by 2003 only 10% of large advertisers paid commissions vs 74% fees), media-buying unbundling in the 1990s, and holding-company consolidation (Interpublic 1961, Omnicom 1986, WPP/Saatchi 1980s).
gaps.why_it_matters: The CREATORS field will be wrong or static for eras 2-7 without this. It also directly serves the centerpiece: AdWords was self-serve — it removed the agency layer for millions of small advertisers, something only legible if the reader knows what the agency layer was charging and how its compensation had already been hollowed out. Media unbundling is also the precondition for programmatic in era 7.
gaps.evidence: HBS working paper 11-039, 'The Unbundling of Advertising Agency Services' (https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/11-039.pdf). ANA agency compensation trend studies (https://www.ana.net/miccontent/show/id/rr-2022-11-ana-trends-in-agency-compensation and https://www.ana.net/content/show/id/440) — commissions at ~10% of large advertisers by 2003, fees dominant since. Marketing Dive on ANA compensation surveys (https://www.marketingdive.com/news/ana-media-commissions-on-upswing-amid-shifting-approach-to-agency-compensa/443314/).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: make agency structure a required thread inside CREATORS for every era (compensation model + industry structure), with the commission's death and holding-company consolidation as EVENTS in eras 3-4 and self-serve disintermediation as an explicit part of era 6's argument.

gaps.title: Below-the-line money (trade promotion, co-op advertising) is invisible, making retail media look new
gaps.claim: By 1990 trade promotion had overtaken media advertising in CPG marketing budgets, and manufacturer-funded co-op advertising (~$10B in 1987, tens of billions today) has flowed through retailers for a century — none of which appears in the plan, even though era 7 presents 'retail media' as an emerging category.
gaps.why_it_matters: Two risks. First, the century chart will implicitly claim to show 'marketing money' while actually showing only measured media, silently excluding a pool that was often larger; historians treat the 1980s advertising-to-promotion budget shift as a major structural story (it is why 'Segmentation'-era measured-media growth slowed). Second, retail media (era 7) is substantially co-op/trade money moving into auction form — Walmart Connect is the descendant of co-op funds — and telling it as a novelty misses the strongest continuity in the whole dataset.
gaps.evidence: HBR, 'The Costly Bargain of Trade Promotion' (1990) (https://hbr.org/1990/03/the-costly-bargain-of-trade-promotion) — documents promotion overtaking advertising in manufacturer budgets. ScienceDirect, Journal of Retailing on manufacturer advertising vs retail promotion (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022435902000660) — advertising's share of promotional budgets declined sharply in the 1980s-90s. Epsilon, 'the $42 billion co-op advertising opportunity' (https://www.epsilon.com/us/insights/blog/the-42-billion-co-op-advertising-opportunity) and Editor & Publisher, 'Co-op advertising: billions hiding in plain sight' (https://www.editorandpublisher.com/stories/revenue-roundup-co-op-advertising,242239).
gaps.recommendation: Add a scoping decision, stated in the methods note: the dataset covers measured advertising media, with a one-paragraph sidebar per relevant era on below-the-line scale; and rewrite era 7's retail-media beat as co-op money changing pricing mechanism (allowance to auction), not a new category.

gaps.title: Pre-1919 misses the trust infrastructure: truth-in-advertising and audited circulation
gaps.claim: Era 1 as scoped (agencies, commission, patent medicines, print) omits the response to patent medicines — Ladies' Home Journal's ad ban (1892), Adams' 'The Great American Fraud' (1905), the Pure Food and Drug Act (1906), the Printers' Ink model statute (1911), the FTC (1914), and the Audit Bureau of Circulations (1914), the world's first audited advertising 'currency.'
gaps.why_it_matters: Historians treat this as the second half of the patent-medicine story: fraud nearly delegitimized the industry, and the trust infrastructure built in response (verified circulation, truth-in-advertising law) is what made national advertising investable. It also opens the plan's best cross-era thread — every era's pricing rests on a trusted measurement currency: audited circulation → Nielsen ratings → impressions → the audited click and quality score. Era 6's auction is the endpoint of a measurement-trust lineage that starts in 1914.
gaps.evidence: History of Information, 'The Audit Bureau of Circulation... is Founded' (https://historyofinformation.com/detail.php?entryid=682) and Ad Age Encyclopedia, 'Audit Bureau of Circulations' (https://adage.com/article/adage-encyclopedia/audit-bureau-circulations/98511). NAAG, 'Evolution of Health Claim Substantiation' (https://www.naag.org/attorney-general-journal/evolution-of-health-claim-substantiation-2/) — LHJ 1892 ban, Adams 1905, Printers' Ink 1911 model statute.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: 3-4 of these as era 1 EVENTS, and add 'measurement currency' as a named cross-era thread that pays off in the era 6 centerpiece.

gaps.title: Era 2's 'Radio' label contradicts the spend data, and WWII's tax-driven advertising is missing
gaps.claim: Newspapers remained the largest US ad medium through the entire 1918-1949 era — radio grew from ~2% of all advertising in 1928 to ~11% in 1932 and never overtook print — so an era named 'Radio' will be contradicted by its own SCALE field; the era also omits the War Advertising Council (1942) and the excess-profits-tax/IRS ruling that made wartime institutional advertising nearly free.
gaps.why_it_matters: The plan cuts eras where the pricing/attention mechanism changed, which radio sponsorship genuinely was — but a reader of the signature chart will see print dominant for the whole era and conclude the chapter title is wrong. The WWII piece is a genuine pricing-mechanism event by the plan's own standard: with a 90% excess-profits tax (Revenue Act of 1942) and the 1942 IRS ruling that goodwill/war-theme ads were deductible, the government effectively subsidized up to ~80% of ad bills, propping up spend when there was nothing to sell and institutionalizing brand advertising.
gaps.evidence: Encyclopedia.com, 'Radio 1929-1941' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/education/news-and-education-magazines/radio-1929-1941) — radio at ~2% (1928) to ~11% (1932) of all advertising. galbithink.org Coen series (https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm) — per-medium series showing print's continued dominance. Wikipedia, 'Ad Council' and 'Revenue Act of 1942' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_Council, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenue_Act_of_1942); hashtagpaid, 'World War II marketing' (https://hashtagpaid.com/banknotes/marketing-through-the-ages-world-war-2) — deductibility subsidizing up to ~80% of ad costs.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure lightly: frame era 2 as 'the broadcast sponsorship model' (mechanism innovation inside a still-print-dominated market) and add the War Advertising Council + 1942 tax ruling to EVENTS/PRICING.

gaps.title: The sponsorship-to-spot transition is a mid-era pricing change era 3 must own
gaps.claim: The mechanism change from sponsor-owned programs to network-controlled programming sold as participating 30-second spots happened inside era 3 (Pat Weaver's magazine concept, early 1950s; cemented by the 1958-59 quiz show scandals), not at an era boundary — the plan lists 'the 30-second spot' as an era 3 feature without the event that created it.
gaps.why_it_matters: By the plan's own cutting rule (eras break where pricing mechanisms change), this is the single biggest pricing-mechanism shift between 1918 and 2002: it moved control of inventory from the advertiser to the network, created scarcity pricing, and made the upfront possible. If era 3's PRICING field doesn't narrate sponsorship's death, the 30-second spot and the upfront appear without a cause, and the parallel to era 6 (platform takes control of inventory, sells fractional units) is lost.
gaps.evidence: Wikipedia, '1950s quiz show scandals' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950s_quiz_show_scandals); PBS American Experience, 'The Aftermath of the Quiz Show Scandal' (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/quizshow-aftermath-quiz-show-scandal/) — networks taking full control of content from sponsors; Encyclopedia.com, 'Quiz Show Scandals' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/media/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/quiz-show-scandals).
gaps.recommendation: Note only (no boundary change needed): require era 3's PRICING and EVENTS fields to carry the sponsorship-to-participation transition explicitly, with the quiz show scandals as the inflection event.

scouts.feasibility_notes: The plan is achievable from this lens, and its data backbone is better than the authors may realize: the Coen/McCann-Erickson series digitized by Douglas Galbi covers 1919-2007 annually with per-medium detail that ALREADY includes direct mail, business papers, Yellow Pages, and a national/local split (galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm; purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/), so most of the categories flagged above cost little extra collection effort — the gaps are scoping choices, not data holes. Three feasibility cautions: (1) Coen ends in 2007 (he retired in 2008); the signature chart requires splicing to IAB/Magna/eMarketer-style series that define media differently (they typically drop direct mail and Yellow Pages and introduce 'digital' as a category that cannibalizes others), so the 1919-2026 chart needs an explicit, documented splice methodology or it will show artifactual breaks around 2007. (2) Pre-1919 there is no annual series; era 1 numbers will be sparse C-grade point estimates (e.g., Printers' Ink-era estimates of a ~$682M market circa 1914), so the plan should state that the chart begins in 1919 while the prose begins in 1833/1840s. (3) The 80% CI + source-grade rigor standard is realistic for 1919-2007 (grade B, single well-documented lineage) but the same number will often have only ONE underlying source (Coen), so CIs there are really judgments about Coen's method — worth saying honestly in the methods note. Finally, adding the recommended money-type split (brand/DR/local/classified) is the highest-leverage change: it reuses data the Coen series already contains and converts the signature chart from 'media shares over time' into direct evidence for the project's central claim about which money Google captured.

scouts.lens: Data archaeologist — existence, provenance, coverage, licensing, and stitch points of long-run US ad-spend datasets

gaps.title: The 1919-2026 'series' is actually two incompatible series with a hard break at 2007/2008
gaps.claim: The canonical long-run series (Printers' Ink -> McCann-Erickson, curated by Robert Coen) ends in December 2008 with final full-year data for 2007. Interpublic replaced it with Magna Global's 'MG8' series, which is a fundamentally different object: media-supplier ad REVENUE built top-down from seller data, versus Coen's bottom-up advertiser BILLINGS built from rate-card list prices. Magna recomputed its methodology back only to 1980. Coen's totals include direct mail, yellow pages, business papers, and a large 'miscellaneous' bucket that successor 'measured media' totals exclude or treat differently, so the levels do not match at the join. A naive splice at 2008 will manufacture a phantom collapse on top of the real Great Recession dip — precisely at the moment the narrative says Google is taking over.
gaps.why_it_matters: The signature chart is the plan's spine. If the join is done naively, the single most-scrutinized visual in the project encodes a measurement artifact as a historical event, and the era-6/7 story ('what Google captured') inherits a wrong baseline.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt, 'Aggregate Advertising Expenditure in the U.S. Economy: What's Up? Is It Real?', NBER Working Paper 28161 (Dec 2020), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf — documents the 2009 discontinuation, the MCE bottom-up billings vs MG8 top-down revenue distinction, MG8 recomputation to 1980 only, and MCE's eleven-media scope incl. direct mail and 'miscellaneous'. Also Douglas Galbi, 'Robert J. Coen, advertising data hero', https://www.purplemotes.net/2009/05/10/robert-j-coen-advertising-data-hero/ (Coen published through Dec 2008).
gaps.recommendation: Restructure: build the data layer as overlapping named series (MCE 1919-2007, MG8 1980-present, IAB internet 1996-present, IRS SOI long-run) with a documented bridge estimated over the 1980-2007 overlap window, and render the signature chart with the overlap visible (two ribbons) rather than one silently spliced line. Add a 'series concordance' object to claims.json.

gaps.title: By-medium detail does not exist before 1935; 1919-1934 media splits are modern reconstructions
gaps.claim: The public Coen data supports a clean by-medium and national/local split only from 1935 onward. For 1919-1934, the freely available Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset's media categories are explicitly a mix of 'some Coen data, some data from other sources, and my own estimates' (Galbi). Worse, the 1920s totals themselves were revised downward about 15% between the 1975 and 2000 vintages of the series. The plan's 'ad-spend-by-medium dataset (1919-2026)' therefore starts 16 years before by-medium data does.
gaps.why_it_matters: The first sixth of the signature chart's stacked-by-medium ribbons would be grade-C reconstruction presented with the same visual authority as the grade-B core, and the radio-era share-shift story (era 2's whole point) rests partly on estimated splits.
gaps.evidence: Douglas Galbi, 'U.S. advertising expenditure data', https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/ (national/local possible from 1935; 1919-1934 categories partly Galbi's own estimates; 1920s figures revised down ~15%); CS Ad Dataset at https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure the chart: total-only line 1919-1934 with by-medium ribbons beginning 1935, or explicitly grade all 1919-1934 medium splits C with wide CIs in claims.json. Do not present 1919-1934 shares at the same confidence as 1935+.

gaps.title: Pre-1919 there is no series at all — only sparse retrospective benchmarks, and nothing before 1867
gaps.claim: The earliest quantitative estimate of total US ad spend is a Printers' Ink retrospective benchmark for 1867 (~$50M), with roughly decennial benchmarks after (1880, 1890, 1900...) — estimates constructed decades after the fact and carried into Historical Statistics of the United States (Millennial Edition Table De482-515, 'Advertising expenditures, by medium: 1867-1998'). For the 1840s-1866 — the first ~25 years of Era 1, including the founding of the first agencies — no credible spend estimate of any kind exists. Additionally, the % of GDP denominator is itself a reconstruction before 1929 (BEA national accounts begin 1929), so pre-1929 ad/GDP ratios are C-grade on both numerator and denominator.
gaps.why_it_matters: Era 1's SCALE field, as specified (total spend, % of GDP, per-medium split, annual with 80% CI), is unfillable as written. If the plan doesn't pre-commit to a benchmark-year format for Era 1, the schema will force fake precision.
gaps.evidence: HSUS Millennial Edition table listing 'Advertising expenditures, by medium: 1867-1998' (De482-515), https://hsus.cambridge.org/HSUSWeb/toc/treeTablePathIdDe482-515.html; Galbi's series and discussion beginning 1919 at https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm and https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/28/more-on-historical-us-advertising-expenditure/. The pre-1919 record consists of benchmark years, not annual data.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure Era 1's SCALE to benchmark years only (1867, 1880, 1890, 1900, 1909, 1914) with wide CIs and an explicitly labeled no-data zone for the 1840s-1866; supplement with Census of Manufactures periodical/newspaper ad receipts (decennial, official) as the only A-grade anchor for the era.

gaps.title: 2008-2026 by-medium data — the stretch the whole project points at — has no free, consistent source
gaps.claim: After Coen ends (2007), every consistent US by-medium series is licensed or paywalled: Magna, GroupM TYNY detail, Zenith, eMarketer, WARC, and the HSUS Millennial Edition itself (Cambridge subscription). The freely citable record for 2008-2026 is a patchwork: IAB/PwC internet ad revenue (1996-2025, free PDFs, US, seller-side), Pew Research newspaper fact sheets (which after 2013 are themselves extrapolations — NAA stopped releasing industry revenue in 2014, and Pew projects the trend from as few as four publicly traded companies' filings), TVB/RAB fragments, and press-release top lines. The plan will be forced into grade-C triangulation for per-medium data in exactly the 18 years it cares most about, or must budget for a license.
gaps.why_it_matters: The centerpiece narrative (what Google captured, then the duopoly/retail-media baseline handed to P3) needs credible per-medium shares for 2008-2026; the plan currently assumes this data is simply available.
gaps.evidence: Pew Newspapers Fact Sheet methodology, https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/fact-sheet/newspapers/ (NAA's last industry figure is 2013; post-2013 estimated from public-company filings); IAB/PwC reports freely archived, e.g. FY2000 report https://www.iab.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/IAB_PWC_002_2000.pdf and 30th-anniversary release https://www.iab.com/news/digital-ad-revenue-climbs-to-nearly-300b-as-iab-celebrates-30-year-anniversary/ ($294.6B US internet ad revenue in 2025); HSUS paywall at https://hsus.cambridge.org/; Baruch College research guide inventorying which ad-expenditure sources are subscription-only, https://guides.newman.baruch.cuny.edu/c.php?g=188246&p=1243745.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: an explicit sourcing decision for 2008-2026 (license one series, or commit to a documented triangulation from IAB + Pew + trade-press top lines + company 10-Ks) and pre-mark those per-medium cells grade B/C in claims.json. Silk & Berndt's appendix tables (free) carry four series through 2018 and can serve as the audited backbone to 2018.

gaps.title: Current-market estimates disagree by tens of billions, driven by definitional scope — especially retail media
gaps.claim: For 2025 alone, eMarketer puts total US ad spending at ~$422B while Magna puts US media-owner ad revenue at ~$398B — a ~$24B gap before you even reach medium splits — and retail media figures diverge wildly by scope (eMarketer: ~$59B US retail media 2025; Magna: $163B for retail media networks on a broader basis). 'Spend' vs 'media-owner revenue', inclusion of agency fees/adtech take, and where retail-media search sits are unreconciled across compilers. There is no single right 2025-2026 number, and any 2026 endpoint is a forecast, not an actual, subject to mid-year revisions (Magna downgraded its 2025 outlook mid-year).
gaps.why_it_matters: Era 7 hands P3 its baseline. If the plan doesn't fix its own definition (advertiser spend vs seller revenue; retail media in or out) before collecting numbers, the 80% CIs will be incoherent — different compilers aren't noisy measurements of one quantity, they measure different quantities.
gaps.evidence: eMarketer, 'US Ad Spending 2025', https://www.emarketer.com/content/us-ad-spending-2025 (~$422B best case); Marketing Dive on Magna's downgraded forecast, https://www.marketingdive.com/news/magna-latest-to-downgrade-global-ad-spending-forecast-expects-979b/750871/ (US media-owner revenue ~$398B, retail media $163B); eMarketer US retail media nearing $70B by 2026, https://www.emarketer.com/chart/c/354785/us-retail-media-ad-spending-will-near-70-billion-2026-354785.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: a one-page measurement concordance (advertiser spend vs media-owner revenue; retail media treatment; agency/adtech take) adopted project-wide before data collection; report era-7 numbers as ranges spanning named compilers; label 2025-2026 points as forecast/preliminary in the signature chart.

gaps.title: The plan's only available A-grade aggregate series — IRS corporate advertising deductions — is not in the plan
gaps.claim: The plan's source-grade A ('official filings') is currently unpopulatable for aggregate ad spend: Coen/MCE is a private agency estimate (B at best), and all successors are commercial estimates. The one long-run official public series — IRS Statistics of Income corporate advertising expense deductions, used in research since Yang (1962) and Telser (1964), e.g. $274.5B for tax year 2012 — is absent from the plan. Silk & Berndt show it correlates r=0.998 with the MCE series over 1960-2007, making it the natural independent validator of the spliced spine, with known caveats (excludes unincorporated firms, includes some promotion, tax-year vs calendar-year timing). The Census Bureau's Service Annual Survey (advertising & marketing services receipts, NAICS-based, annual from ~1998-2001) is a second official cross-check.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without an official anchor, every number in the century dataset traces to one agency economist's estimates and their commercial successors; with IRS SOI, the plan gets an A-grade validation rail and an honest answer to 'how do you know Coen wasn't making it up'.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt, NBER WP 28161, Section III.2.1 and Figure 3 (IRS series description, $274.504B for 2012, r=0.998 with MCE 1960-2007, SAS8 description), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf; companion IARIW version https://iariw.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/ernst_paper.pdf.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope + collect data: pull IRS SOI advertising-deduction totals as a parallel validation series in claims.json, and use divergence between IRS and the media series as a feature (it measures below-the-line/promotion drift), not a bug.

gaps.title: The Coen numbers are rate-card billings, not transaction prices — which collides with the plan's own PRICING story
gaps.claim: The MCE estimates were built from list ('rate card') prices, not the discounted transaction prices actually paid — Silk & Berndt state the estimates were 'typically based on information about current list prices... rather than actual transaction prices that reflected volume and other discounts.' A project whose analytical spine is 'who set the price in each era' (commission -> rate card -> upfront -> CPM -> auction) will be quoting SCALE numbers from a dataset that systematically embeds unmeasured, era-varying discounting — heaviest exactly where negotiation was heaviest (TV scatter, late-era newspapers).
gaps.why_it_matters: It caps the source grade of the entire 1919-2007 spine at B, and it means medium shares are distorted relative to true money flows in eras where discounting off rate card differed by medium — a subtle but real bias in the era 3-5 share-shift story.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt, NBER WP 28161, Section III.2.2, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf.
gaps.recommendation: Note in methodology and in the PRICING field of each era: the flagship series measures list-price billings; grade MCE-derived numbers B; where the prose makes a pricing-mechanism claim, do not cite the spend dataset as if it recorded realized prices.

gaps.title: 'One global market-size figure per era' is impossible for Era 1 and barely sourced before the 1960s
gaps.claim: No global advertising market estimate exists for the 1840s-1917 period at all. The earliest recurring global source is the 'Survey of World Advertising Expenditures' lineage (International Advertising Association, founded 1938, later compiled by Starch INRA Hooper), a print publication held in libraries, not online — one edition (1990) is freely available via UNESCO. Consistent commercial global series (Zenith, Magna, GroupM, WARC) begin in the 1980s and are licensed. So the plan's per-era global figure is: Era 1 nonexistent, Era 2 a single late-era print benchmark at best, Eras 3-4 library archaeology, Eras 5-7 paywalled or press-release top lines.
gaps.why_it_matters: A schema cell the plan treats as routine is unfillable for the first era and C-grade until roughly the 1960s; better to know now than to discover it mid-writing.
gaps.evidence: ISSN record for 'Survey of world advertising expenditures' (Starch INRA Hooper/IAA), https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/0894-5004; IAA founding 1938, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Advertising_Association; UNESCO-hosted 1990 world survey, https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000094735.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure the schema rule: global figure required only from Era 3 onward; Era 1 marked 'no data exists'; Era 2 allowed a single benchmark-year figure. Budget one library/ILL retrieval for the Starch INRA Hooper volumes if global numbers for eras 3-4 must be sourced rather than triangulated.

gaps.title: Front-edge no-data zones inside eras 2 and 5, and a forecast-only endpoint at 2026
gaps.claim: Era 2 opens in 1918, but radio advertising did not exist until 1922 (WEAF toll broadcasting) and no radio spend data exists before the late 1920s (structured by-medium data only from 1935). Era 5 opens in 1994 (HotWired banner, October 1994), but the IAB/PwC series begins with 1996; 1994-1995 web ad revenue exists only as anecdote and one-off estimates. And the chart's 2026 endpoint can only ever be a forecast at publication time. Each era's opening years — narratively the most dramatized — are the least measurable.
gaps.why_it_matters: The prose will naturally want numbers at each era's dramatic opening ('radio arrives', 'the banner ad debuts'); the data layer cannot supply them, inviting exactly the ungraded improvised figures the rigor rules exist to prevent.
gaps.evidence: IAB 30th-anniversary release confirming the report series began in 1996, https://www.iab.com/news/digital-ad-revenue-climbs-to-nearly-300b-as-iab-celebrates-30-year-anniversary/; Galbi on by-medium detail from 1935, https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/; supplementary monthly Printers' Ink advertising activity INDEX (not dollars) from 1919 exists on FRED for texture, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/M0658BUSM343SNBR.
gaps.recommendation: Note only: pre-authorize 'no credible data' as a legitimate schema value for 1918-1926 radio, 1994-1995 web, and mark 2026 as forecast in the chart legend and claims.json as-of dates.

gaps.title: The 'advertising is always ~2% of GDP' folklore is contested — treat the ad/GDP ratio as a finding, not an assumption
gaps.claim: The often-repeated claim that US advertising has been a constant share of GDP for a century is disputed in the very literature the plan will rely on: Silk & Berndt open with dueling 2014-2019 claims of constancy versus decline, and estimate that the elasticity of ad spend with respect to GDP broke structurally in the late 1990s (from ~1.4 to ~1.9), coincident with digital's rise. Different series (IRS vs MCE vs MG8) give different ad/GDP levels and trends. If the SCALE field's %-of-GDP row is filled from whichever series is at hand per era, the century chart will imply a constancy or a decline that is an artifact of series-switching.
gaps.why_it_matters: The %-of-GDP framing is the plan's cross-era comparability device; it is also precisely where the measurement literature says naive use misleads — and the late-1990s elasticity break is itself a better headline for the Google story than the folklore constancy.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt, NBER WP 28161, abstract and Section I (Bloomberg 'always about 1 percent' claim vs brokerage 'declining share' claim; elasticity 1.4 -> 1.9 break), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf.
gaps.recommendation: Note only: compute %-of-GDP from one declared series per stretch, footnote the series switch, and consider promoting the late-1990s elasticity break into the era 5/6 narrative — it is quantitative evidence that the Google era changed the size of the pie, not just its division.

scouts.feasibility_notes: The signature chart is feasible, but only as a documented patchwork, never as the single continuous series the plan currently implies. The freely citable backbone is: (1) the Coen/McCann-Erickson series 1919-2007, publicly mirrored as Galbi's Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset (galbithink.org, downloadable xls) with by-medium detail solid only from 1935; (2) IAB/PwC internet ad revenue 1996-2025 (free PDFs); (3) IRS SOI corporate advertising deductions as the only official long-run validator; (4) Silk & Berndt's NBER WP 28161 appendix tables carrying four reconciled series 1960-2018 — this paper is effectively a prefabricated methodology chapter and should be read before any data collection. Pre-1919 is benchmark-years-only (1867 earliest; nothing before), and 2008-2026 by-medium requires either a commercial license (Magna/eMarketer/WARC) or committed grade-C triangulation from IAB + Pew + press top lines + 10-Ks. Two schema amendments are needed for honesty: benchmark-year format for Era 1 SCALE, and 'no credible data' as a legal cell value. Expect roughly: grade A only for IRS/Census cross-checks and company filings (Google S-1/10-Ks, Overture 10-Ks); grade B for the 1935-2007 Coen core and IAB; grade C for 1919-1934 medium splits, all pre-1919 points, most global figures before the 1980s, and 2008-2026 per-medium unless licensed. Budget one series-concordance/bridge-factor task (1980-2007 MCE-MG8 overlap) before chart-building; it is the single highest-leverage piece of data work in the project.

scouts.lens: Google mechanics analyst — what the auction-centric story of Google's capture misses or gets wrong against the 1998-2008 record

gaps.title: Distribution deals, not auction design, were the decisive capture lever — and a federal court agrees
gaps.claim: The plan's centerpiece attributes Google's capture to AdRank + AdSense, but the historical record shows distribution/syndication was at least co-equal: Yahoo made Google its default search provider in June 2000 (before AdWords Select existed), the May 2002 AOL deal (a bet-the-company $100M revenue guarantee with 85% rev share) flipped the market against Overture overnight, network/partner sites were still 41% of Google revenue in 2006 with TAC at 32% of ad revenue, and Judge Mehta's August 2024 ruling found Google maintained its search monopoly specifically through exclusive default-distribution payments (e.g., to Apple), not through auction superiority.
gaps.why_it_matters: Overture HAD the keyword auction first and was the revenue leader through 2002; it lost on distribution and owned-destination traffic. If the chapter's worked-numbers argument says 'the quality-weighted auction is why Google won,' it tells a mechanism story the record flunks — the auction explains yield per query, distribution explains query volume, and capture required both.
gaps.evidence: Google press archive, 'Yahoo! Selects Google as its Default Search Engine Provider' (June 2000): http://googlepress.blogspot.com/2000/06/yahoo-selects-google-as-its-default.html; Search Engine Watch, 'Overture & Inktomi Out, Google In At AOL' (2002): https://www.searchenginewatch.com/2002/04/30/overture-inktomi-out-google-in-at-aol/; TheStreet, 'Overture Plunges 37% on Partnership Worries': https://www.thestreet.com/technology/overture-plunges-37-on-partnership-worries-10020364; Google Q2 2006 press release via SEC (network = 41% of revenue, TAC = 32%): https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1288776/000119312506150132/dex991.htm; Fortune on Mehta remedies ruling re exclusive distribution deals: https://fortune.com/2025/09/02/google-antitrust-remedy-ruling-exclusive-search-distribution-deals-chrome/
gaps.recommendation: Restructure era 6: make the centerpiece a twin-engine story (auction = yield, distribution = volume) with the AOL-deal economics and TAC/network-share as calibrated numbers in SCALE/SELLERS; add the 2024 Mehta ruling to era 7 EVENTS as the retrospective verdict on which lever mattered.

gaps.title: Search's money came from classifieds, Yellow Pages, and direct response — not TV brand budgets — and directories are likely missing from the signature chart
gaps.claim: The first budgets search took were newspaper classifieds (US peak $19.6B in 2000, down to $4.6B by 2012; help-wanted alone fell >90% from $8.7B to $723M), Yellow Pages/directories (peak $14.7B in 2005, $3.2B by 2015), and direct-response/lead-gen categories (mortgage, travel, eBay-style marketplaces) — TV brand budgets held for another decade. A century-long ad-spend-by-medium dataset that lacks a 'directories/classifieds' line will mismeasure exactly the transfer the project exists to explain.
gaps.why_it_matters: The project's core question is 'what did Google capture and from whom.' If eras 6-7 imply capture from mass-media brand spend, the BUYERS story is wrong: search monetized bottom-of-funnel intent money that had lived in classifieds, directories, and direct mail — media the plan's era schema barely names. Yellow Pages was a ~$14B market that appears nowhere in the seven era titles.
gaps.evidence: Poynter, 'Classified Ad Revenue Down 70 Percent in 10 Years' (NAA data): https://www.poynter.org/reporting-editing/2010/classified-ad-revenue-down-70-percent-in-10-years-with-one-bright-spot/; Congressional Research Service, 'Stop the Presses? Newspapers in the Digital Age' (2022): https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R47018/R47018.2.pdf; The Quota, 'The Rise (and Fall) of Yellow Pages Sales' ($14.7B peak 2005): https://www.thequota.co/articles/the-rise-and-fall-of-yellow-pages-sales; AdMarketplace (eBay's exclusive search ad platform 2003-2006, direct-response archetype): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AdMarketplace
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: (1) a 'directories + classifieds' medium line in the 1919-2026 dataset (Coen/McCann historical series carries Yellow Pages as a line item); (2) era 6 BUYERS must name the source-of-funds categories (classifieds, directories, direct mail, lead gen) with the collapse curves as calibrated numbers; (3) era 6-7 must state explicitly that TV brand budgets migrated later, via programmatic/video, not via 2000s search.

gaps.title: The schema has TARGETING but no MEASUREMENT — the attribution loop that moved the money is structurally invisible
gaps.claim: The fixed 8-field schema cannot express the single biggest thing advertisers gained in the Google era: closed-loop ROI proof. Conversion tracking plus the Urchin acquisition (March 2005, ~$30M) rebranded as free Google Analytics (Nov 2005) — which ended paid web analytics as a market 'overnight' — let advertisers justify rising CPCs with per-keyword conversion data. Measurement is also era-defining backwards: ABC circulation audits (1914), Nielsen ratings, direct-mail coupon codes, CPM 'proof' by panel — every era's pricing power rested on what buyers could verify.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without a measurement field, era 6 can only say 'auction set the price,' not 'advertisers could finally prove value, which is why they tolerated the price' — and the era-by-era comparison loses the thread (audit -> ratings -> CTR -> conversion) that explains why each pricing regime was believable enough to move budgets. Google's free-analytics move was a deliberate mechanism to raise willingness-to-pay in its own auction, i.e., part of the capture machinery the plan credits to the auction alone.
gaps.evidence: Search Engine Watch, 'Google To Acquire Urchin' (2005): https://www.searchenginewatch.com/2005/03/29/google-to-acquire-urchin-web-analytics-firm/; Primo Interactive, 'The history of Google Analytics: from Urchin to GA4' (free launch Nov 14 2005, sign-ups closed within a week, paid analytics market collapse): https://www.primointeractive.com/blog/history-of-google-analytics; Crunchbase blog, 'The Urchin Software Mafia': https://about.crunchbase.com/blog/san-diego-tech-company-urchin
gaps.recommendation: Restructure: add a ninth schema field, MEASUREMENT (what the buyer could verify: circulation audit -> ratings/demos -> reach/frequency -> CTR -> conversion/attribution), applied to all seven eras; put Urchin/GA and AdWords conversion tracking in era 6 EVENTS.

gaps.title: Self-serve with no minimums and automated review expanded WHO could advertise — market creation, not just capture
gaps.claim: Google's removal of friction (self-serve signup from Oct 2000, $0.05 minimum bids from Feb 2002, automated ad approval) versus Overture's model (human editorial review with 3-5 day listing approval, minimum deposits/bids) created millions of long-tail small-business advertisers who had never bought media through an agency at all — AdWords went from ~350 advertisers at launch to a base where small advertisers collectively out-spent large ones. The plan's framing ('what let Google capture so much of it') misses that a large share of search revenue was net-new demand that no prior medium ever held.
gaps.why_it_matters: This changes the CREATORS/BUYERS story for era 6 (no agency, no commission, advertiser writes own text ad — the 15% commission thread from era 1 dies here, a structural bookend the plan should land) and changes the SCALE math: total-market growth vs share transfer must be decomposed or the century chart will overstate 'capture.'
gaps.evidence: Search Engine Watch, 'How Overture (GoTo) Works' (editorial review, funding minimums): https://www.searchenginewatch.com/2002/03/04/how-overture-goto-works/; PPC Hero, 'A History of Google AdWords' (350 advertisers Oct 2000; $0.05 CPC minimums Feb 2002): https://ppchero.com/a-history-of-google-adwords-and-google-ads-revolutionizing-digital-advertising-marketing-since-2000/; ACT | The App Association, 'The Long Tail of Advertising' (small advertisers at heart of Google's base): https://actonline.org/2011/09/15/the-long-tail-of-advertising-small-business-advertisers-at-the-heart-of-ftcs-google-probe/; VentureBeat, 'Google and the Long Tail': https://venturebeat.com/business/google-and-the-long-tail
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: era 6 needs an advertiser-count series (will be grade B/C — Google disclosed sparingly) and an explicit expansion-vs-capture decomposition; tie the death of the 15% agency commission for this buyer class back to era 1 as a deliberate narrative bookend.

gaps.title: 1998-2008 timeline corrections: AdWords launched as CPM, Overture led revenue through 2002, and Google paid ~$300M for the model it 'improved'
gaps.claim: Three record-level facts the plan's era structure currently blurs: (a) AdWords at launch (Oct 23, 2000) was self-serve CPM, not an auction — the CPC auction arrived as 'AdWords Select' in Feb 2002, so 'the auction era starts 2002' is right but 'AdWords = auction' is not; (b) Overture, not Google, was the paid-search revenue leader into 2002 ($667.7M FY2002 revenue, 2.2B paid introductions) — Google's design didn't win in the market until distribution flipped; (c) Google settled Overture's patent suit 10 days before its 2004 IPO for 2.7M shares (~$300M at IPO; Yahoo later sold them for ~$1.5B) — an explicit price tag on how much of the mechanism was inherited rather than invented.
gaps.why_it_matters: The centerpiece chapter's credibility rests on getting 'what Google actually added' exactly right: what Google added was CTR-weighting (expected-revenue ranking), next-price billing, no minimum spend, and automation on top of GoTo's 1998 keyword-bid + PPC + advertiser-funded-ranking invention. Misdating AdWords or omitting the patent settlement invites easy debunking of the whole chapter.
gaps.evidence: PPC Hero AdWords history (Oct 2000 CPM launch, ~350 advertisers; Feb 2002 AdWords Select CPC): https://ppchero.com/a-history-of-google-adwords-and-google-ads-revolutionizing-digital-advertising-marketing-since-2000/; Overture Services FY2002 10-K (SEC, $667.7M revenue): https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1060439/000095014803000429/v88074e10vk.htm; DWW, 'Google Transfers 2.7 Million Shares to Yahoo in Settlement': https://www.dww.com/articles/google-transfers-27-million-shares-to-yahoo-settlement-of-a-search-patent-dispute; NBC News, 'Google boosts IPO after settling with rival': https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna5650780; Slate, 'How Bill Gross' GoTo.com inspired AdWords': https://slate.com/business/2013/10/googles-big-break-how-bill-gross-goto-com-inspired-the-adwords-business-model.html
gaps.recommendation: Collect data / correct: era 6 EVENTS must carry Oct-2000 (CPM AdWords), Feb-2002 (AdWords Select CPC auction), May-2002 (AOL), Aug-2004 (Overture patent settlement); era 5 should carry Overture's revenue lead as a calibrated number so the crossover is visible.

gaps.title: The GSP auction was not a fixed mechanism — Google tuned pricing knobs (squashing, format pricing, RGSP) to hit revenue targets
gaps.claim: DOJ v. Google trial evidence (2023-24) shows the search auction the simulator will canonize was progressively overridden once Google had market power: 'squashing' artificially inflated the runner-up's predicted CTR to raise the winner's price, format pricing and other 'knobs' were used for 'intentional pricing,' auction changes routinely raised prices ~5% per Google ads VP Jerry Dischler's testimony, and RGSP (randomized GSP, 2019) — which sometimes lets the second-ranked bidder win to push bids upward — raised revenue ~10%. The elegant bid-times-quality second-price story is accurate for ~2002-2010 and increasingly false afterward.
gaps.why_it_matters: If the interactive simulator teaches 'quality-weighted GSP beats pure bid' as a timeless design truth, it will present as Google's enduring mechanism something Google itself abandoned in pieces for revenue extraction — and the P3 handoff ('why isn't advertising solving AI economics') inherits a falsely benign model of auction-funded free services. It also sharpens the framing: bid × pCTR ranking is expected-revenue-per-impression maximization, not relevance altruism.
gaps.evidence: Search Engine Land, 'How Google harms search advertisers in 20 slides' (DOJ exhibits: squashing, pricing knobs, intentional pricing): https://searchengineland.com/doj-google-search-ad-price-manipulation-440207; Search Engine Land, 'What is RGSP? Google's Randomized Generalized Second-Price ad auctions explained': https://searchengineland.com/google-rgsp-randomized-generalized-second-price-ad-auctions-explained-433053; MoreVisibility, 'Google Admits to Tweaking Advertising Auctions for Revenue Goals' (Dischler testimony, ~5%): https://www.morevisibility.com/paid-media/insights/google-admits-to-tweaking-advertising-auctions-for-revenue-goals/
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: a 'the auction gets knobs' beat in era 7 (with the DOJ trial as an EVENTS entry) and, ideally, a simulator toggle demonstrating squashing/RGSP so the reader sees how a 'second-price' auction becomes a price-setting instrument under monopoly; frame AdRank in era 6 as expected-revenue ranking from the start.

gaps.title: April 2004 trademark-keyword policy change: a deliberate revenue unlock the EVENTS list should carry
gaps.claim: In April 2004 Google reversed policy and let third parties bid on trademarked terms as keywords, triggering GEICO v. Google (E.D. Va. 2004, ruling that keyword sale itself was lawful, settled Sept 2005) — a quiet mechanism change that turned brand names into auctionable inventory and forced brand owners to bid on their own names, a pure price-of-entry revenue stream the auction-design story never mentions.
gaps.why_it_matters: It is a concrete example of Google unilaterally expanding what counts as sellable inventory — a recurring pattern (broad match, close variants) that explains revenue growth independent of query growth or auction design, and it sets up the era-7 pattern of quiet inventory/matching expansions.
gaps.evidence: The Register, 'Judge clarifies Google AdWords ruling' (April 2004 policy change, GEICO suit): https://www.theregister.com/2005/08/15/google_loses_adwords_trademark_case/; GEICO v. Google, 330 F. Supp. 2d 700 (E.D. Va. 2004), Justia: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp2/330/700/2314271/
gaps.recommendation: Note only: add to era 6 EVENTS (April 2004 policy change + GEICO ruling) and flag 'inventory-definition expansion' as a named mechanism alongside the auction.

scouts.feasibility_notes: The era-6 centerpiece is achievable at the plan's rigor bar, but only if it becomes a multi-mechanism chapter: the auction math is well documented, and — unusually for this project — the counterweight evidence is grade A (Overture's 10-K revenue on SEC EDGAR, Google's SEC-filed quarterly network/TAC splits, the Overture patent settlement in Google's S-1/A, and DOJ trial exhibits for the auction-knobs story). Two data risks: (1) an AdWords advertiser-count time series was never systematically disclosed, so the market-expansion claim will rest on B/C-grade triangulation (In the Plex, FTC-probe reporting, scattered Google statements); (2) the signature 1919-2026 chart needs a directories/classified line — the Coen/McCann historical series carries Yellow Pages and newspaper-classified splits only patchily, so budget collection time for splicing NAA classified data (2000-2012) and Yellow Pages association data onto it. The single biggest planning risk is narrative, not data: as scoped, the chapter argues 'better auction won,' while the record shows the auction leader of 2002 (Overture) losing to distribution, self-serve scale, and measurement — write the centerpiece as 'yield engine (auction) times volume engine (distribution) times belief engine (measurement)' and every finding above slots in rather than contradicts.

scouts.lens: Contrarian fact-checker — where the "eras evolved, then Google's superior auction ate the market" story is contested, mythical, or contradicted by the long-run data

gaps.title: The 'capture' premise is contested: measured US ad/GDP peaked in 2000 and FELL during Google's rise
gaps.claim: US advertising as a share of GDP was not constant at ~2% and did not expand when digital arrived: the McCann-Erickson (MCE) and IRS series both peak in 2000 at 2.3-2.4% of GDP and then drop below 2% through 2007/2014 — exactly the AdWords years — while the 1920s sat near 2.8-2.9% and a widely-cited 2014 Bloomberg piece claims the industry 'has always been about 1 percent of GDP'. Which series you pick reverses the story.
gaps.why_it_matters: The project's core question — 'what did Google capture' — presupposes a stable pie being redivided. The authoritative NBER study (Silk & Berndt 2020) frames this as an open question: 'a growth problem, a measurement problem, or both?', finding the GDP-elasticity of ad spend structurally broke in the late 1990s (~1.4 to ~1.9) while four canonical series (IRS, MCE, Magna, Census SAS) materially disagree. If the plan asserts one ad/GDP line, the adversarial-verification stage will find a credible source contradicting it. The deeper issue: much of Google's revenue came from money never counted as 'advertising' (Yellow Pages, classifieds, co-op, below-the-line promotion — IRS 'advertising' expense itself mixes in promotion), so capture vs reallocation vs measurement-boundary-shift must be adjudicated, not assumed.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt, 'Aggregate Advertising Expenditure in the U.S. Economy: What's Up? Is It Real?', NBER WP 28161 (Dec 2020), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf — read directly: MCE/IRS shares peak 2000 at 2.3%/2.4% then fall below 2%; elasticity break late 1990s; quotes Bloomberg 2014 'always been about 1 percent of U.S. GDP' vs Telser's stable-share tradition; notes IRS 'advertising' likely includes consumer and trade promotion. Galbi, 'US Annual Advertising Spending Since 1919', https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm — ~2.8% of GDP late 1920s, ~1.8% 1970s, ~2.2-2.3% 1990s-2000s.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure: make 'the ad intensity of the economy' an explicit cross-era analytical thread with its own chapter-level answer. Show the competing series side by side (never merged), take a documented stance on capture-vs-reallocation-vs-boundary-shift, and put the Silk & Berndt four-series comparison in the source base now. Add a boundary statement to the SCALE field definition (measured media advertising vs promotion vs total marketing).

gaps.title: The signature 1919-2026 chart cannot be one series — the splice seams are large and documented
gaps.claim: No continuous by-medium US ad-spend series 1919-2026 exists. The Coen/McCann series ends in 2007 and was discontinued by IPG in 2009; its replacement (Magna Global) uses a fundamentally different methodology (top-down media-supplier revenue vs Coen's bottom-up billings built on rate-card LIST prices, not transaction prices) and was backcast only to 1980. Category breaks are material: 'Out of Home' replaced 'Billboards' in 2000 at roughly 3x the expenditure; TV split into broadcast/cable in 1990; pre-1940 Coen figures were revised downward ~15% over the years; 'miscellaneous' was ~20% of the 1935 total.
gaps.why_it_matters: The century chart is the flagship deliverable. If it is drawn as one line per medium, the adversarial-verification stage will show that the 1990s-2000s digital-vs-traditional comparison mixes rate-card billings with supplier net revenue (IAB internet numbers are revenue; Coen print numbers are list-price billings), and that apparent inflections (OOH 2000, TV 1990) are definitional artifacts. The chart's credibility — and every claims.json entry hanging off it — dies.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt NBER WP 28161, pp. 7-9 (MCE based on 'list' rate-card prices not transaction prices; IPG discontinued MCE in 2009; Magna 'fundamental departure', backcast to 1980), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf. Purple Motes, 'U.S. advertising expenditure data', https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/ — OOH 2000 3x break, 1990 TV split, pre-1940 downward revisions ~15%, miscellaneous ~20% (1935).
gaps.recommendation: Restructure the deliverable: design the chart as explicitly spliced segments with visible seam annotations and a methodology panel; carry source-series and definition per data point in claims.json; render billings-based and revenue-based segments in distinguishable treatments. Budget data-engineering time for a splice audit (overlap years 1980-2007 where Coen and Magna coexist).

gaps.title: The centerpiece's causal claim — 'the auction design won' — is the most contested claim in the plan
gaps.claim: Google's victory is at least as attributable to distribution economics and scale as to auction design: (a) Overture invented the pay-per-click keyword auction (Patent 6,269,361) and Google settled the infringement suit for 2.7M shares (~$229.5M at IPO price); (b) Google took AOL from Overture in May 2002 with a $100M revenue guarantee and 85% rev-share — a balance-sheet risk bet, not a mechanism-design win; (c) Google paid Apple ~$20B in 2022 alone (36% of Safari search ad revenue) for default placement, and Judge Mehta's August 2024 ruling found monopoly maintained through exclusive distribution defaults — not through auction quality; (d) 2023 DOJ trial testimony (Jerry Dischler) revealed Google routinely tuned the auction with undisclosed 'pricing knobs' — squashing, format pricing, and RGSP (2019) — raising prices ~5-10% without quality improvement, undermining the 'elegant neutral mechanism' framing.
gaps.why_it_matters: As scoped, era 6 proves 'why this design beats pure bid' with worked numbers. That proves the mechanism is clever; it does not prove the mechanism caused the win. Overture ran the 'inferior' pure-bid auction profitably and raised its 2002 guidance even after losing AOL — it died from losing distribution, not from auction inefficiency. If the chapter's thesis is 'better auction → market capture', the adversarial stage will produce the DOJ record and the Overture history as refutation. There is also a live inversion: the quality-weighted auction Google runs today is demonstrably not the textbook GSP the simulator will teach.
gaps.evidence: Google 10-K FY2004 (Overture/Yahoo settlement, 2.7M shares, $229.5M), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001288776/000119312505065298/d10k.htm; Slate, 'Google's big break: How Bill Gross' GoTo.com inspired AdWords', https://slate.com/business/2013/10/googles-big-break-how-bill-gross-goto-com-inspired-the-adwords-business-model.html; Search Engine Watch, 'Overture & Inktomi Out, Google In At AOL' (May 2002), https://www.searchenginewatch.com/2002/04/30/overture-inktomi-out-google-in-at-aol/; The Register, 'Google's AOL win upsets Inktomi, Overture', https://www.theregister.com/2002/05/02/googles_aol_win_upsets_inktomi/; CNBC on Mehta remedies and $26B default deals, https://www.cnbc.com/2025/08/27/google-search-antitrust-decision-apple.html; AppleInsider on the ruling ending exclusivity, https://appleinsider.com/articles/25/09/02/google-must-stop-exclusive-contracts-with-companies-like-apple-but-keeps-chrome; Search Engine Land, 'How Google harms search advertisers in 20 slides' (squashing, RGSP, format pricing, +5-10%), https://searchengineland.com/doj-google-search-ad-price-manipulation-440207.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure era 6's thesis from 'the auction won the market' to 'the auction solved the pricing problem; distribution, guarantees, and scale won the market'. Keep the simulator and worked numbers, but add: (1) a TAC/distribution-economics section with the AOL 2002 and Apple numbers; (2) an Overture post-mortem showing the pure-bid auction was profitable and lost on distribution; (3) a coda on the DOJ pricing-knob evidence showing the deployed auction diverged from the textbook mechanism. Front-load these sources before drafting.

gaps.title: Traditional media did not collapse when digital arrived — and what collapsed was not TV
gaps.claim: The substitution timeline contradicts a 'digital arrived (1994), traditional fell' arc: US newspaper ad revenue PEAKED in 2005 (~$49B, a decade after the banner ad), with classifieds peaking in 2000; TV's share of media receipts ROSE through the entire AdWords era to a ~35% peak in 2014, and TV dollars peaked in 2018 ($72.4B); digital passed TV as the largest medium only in 2016. The media Google's search actually gutted were the direct-response ones: directories/Yellow Pages (~9% share in 1991 to <1% by 2018), newspapers (37% in 1980 to 4% in 2018, classifieds first, driven partly by Craigslist and the 2001 recession before Google's auction mattered), and direct mail (lost a third of its 12% share).
gaps.why_it_matters: Eras 5-7 will tell a false displacement story if 'Google captured advertising' is illustrated with TV-era brand budgets. Search competed for direct-response and local money (classifieds, directories, direct mail); social later competed for brand money. Without this distinction the era 6-7 chapters misattribute newspaper deaths to the auction and miss that TV was untouched for 20 years — which is also the single most interesting fact the signature chart will show.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt NBER WP 28161, Figures 4-5 discussion (TV share 28% in 1996, peak ~35% in 2014; newspapers 37%→4% 1980-2018; directories ~9% 1991→<1% 2018; direct mail -1/3 of 12%), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf; MediaPost/eMarketer, 'U.S. TV Ad Spending Has Peaked' (2018 peak $72.4B), https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/343267/; CJR, 'Craigslist = Straw Man' (classifieds peaked 2000; held through 2006), https://www.cjr.org/short_takes/craigslist_straw_man_1.php; MinnPost, 'How Craigslist killed the newspapers' golden goose', http://www.minnpost.com/business/2014/02/how-craigslist-killed-newspapers-golden-goose/; Benedict Evans, 'News by the ton: 75 years of US advertising', https://www.ben-evans.com/benedictevans/2020/6/14/75-years-of-us-advertising.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: a 'who actually lost, and when' analysis in eras 6-7 keyed to the by-medium data, with directories and classifieds as the primary victims and TV's 2014/2018 peaks stated explicitly. Treat Craigslist/classifieds as an EVENTS entry in era 6 independent of Google.

gaps.title: The 8-field schema lacks the axis the whole story turns on: national/brand vs local/direct-response
gaps.claim: Every serious historical series (Coen classified all eleven media national vs local; Magna classifies Direct/National/Local) splits ad spend by national-brand vs local/direct-response — and Google's capture maps almost entirely onto the local/direct-response half (classifieds, directories, direct mail, co-op). The plan's schema (BUYERS/SELLERS/MEDIUM/SCALE/PRICING/TARGETING) has no field that carries this split, so the mechanism of substitution is inexpressible in the data layer.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without this axis, era chapters can state totals but cannot explain flows: why newspapers (60%+ local/classified revenue) died while TV (national brand) didn't; why search CPC budgets came from Yellow Pages and direct mail lines, not TV upfronts; why the P3 handoff question (performance ads funding zero-price services) is really about the direct-response pool. It also protects against the classic apples-to-oranges error of comparing search (pure direct response) to 'advertising' writ large.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt NBER WP 28161, p.7 (MCE's eleven media each classified national vs local) and Magna's Direct/National/Local typology, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf; Benedict Evans, 'News by the ton' (newspaper revenue composition: classified/local retail vs national), https://www.ben-evans.com/benedictevans/2020/6/14/75-years-of-us-advertising.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure the schema: add a ninth field or a mandated sub-split of BUYERS/SCALE into brand vs direct-response (national vs local as the historical proxy), with a share estimate + CI per era. This is cheap now and impossible to retrofit after chapters are drafted.

gaps.title: Era 1 (1840s-1917) cannot meet the stated rigor bar — there is no annual data before 1919
gaps.claim: The Coen dataset begins in 1919; pre-1919 aggregates (e.g., 1865-1867 estimates, Printers' Ink-style figures) are decadal guesses that the dataset's own curators flag as questionable, and even Coen's pre-1940 numbers were revised downward ~15% over time. An 80% CI + source-grade + as-of-date SCALE entry for the 1840s-1910s will be false precision, and the 'signature chart 1919-2026' already concedes this by silently excluding 75 years of era 1.
gaps.why_it_matters: The fixed schema applied uniformly will force fabricated confidence exactly where the record is thinnest, and the adversarial stage will flag it. The mismatch between era 1's start (1840s) and the chart's start (1919) is currently unexplained in the plan and will read as an error.
gaps.evidence: Galbi, 'US Annual Advertising Spending Since 1919' (series begins 1919; no pre-1919 data), https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm; Purple Motes (skepticism about 1865-1867 aggregates; pre-1940 revisions ~15%), https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope a declared 'degraded rigor mode' for pre-1919: decadal point estimates only, grade C mandatory, order-of-magnitude CIs, and an explicit note in the chart and prose that the annual record starts in 1919. Do not let the schema force annual numbers before then.

gaps.title: Era names imply spend dominance the data will contradict: radio was never #1, and newspapers out-earned TV deep into the 'TV era'
gaps.claim: Radio never became the largest US ad medium — newspapers remained #1 by total dollars throughout 1918-1949 (the oft-repeated '1938: radio overtook print' claim refers to magazines, not all print); and during the 1950-1975 'TV Mass Market' era newspapers still out-earned TV in total dollars (newspapers were 37% of media receipts as late as 1980, vs TV's 28% as late as 1996) — TV led national brand advertising, not total advertising. Digital likewise didn't pass TV until 2016, well into 'era 7'.
gaps.why_it_matters: Each era's SCALE field must report the per-medium split; if the chapter titles say 'Radio' and 'TV Mass Market' while the era's own table shows newspapers as the largest line, readers and reviewers will see a contradiction. The mid-century claims ('by 1954/1955 TV was the leading medium') circulating in secondary sources are about national advertising and are routinely misquoted as totals — a myth the project should pre-empt rather than repeat.
gaps.evidence: Silk & Berndt NBER WP 28161 (newspapers 37% of media receipts in 1980; TV 28% in 1996; digital supplanted TV only in 2016), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf; Coen dataset via Galbi, https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm; conflicting secondary claims, e.g. Wikipedia 'History of advertising' ('1938 radio surpassed print') https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_advertising vs Smithsonian/ANA-derived '1954 TV leading medium' claims, https://americanhistory.si.edu/explore/exhibitions/american-enterprise/online/advertising-business/madison-avenue.
gaps.recommendation: Note in the plan: era names denote the era's pricing/attention innovation, not the largest medium — and require each era's SCALE field to name the actual #1 medium by total dollars (with the national-vs-local caveat). Verify radio's true peak share (~mid-teens, mid-1940s) against the Coen by-medium file during data collection.

gaps.title: Myth inventory to pre-clear: the Wanamaker quote and the 'first banner ad' are both shaky
gaps.claim: Two near-certain chapter anecdotes are compromised: (1) 'Half the money I spend on advertising is wasted...' has no primary-source citation to John Wanamaker — Quote Investigator's earliest attribution is a 1919 sermon, and the line is also credited to Lord Leverhulme, Wrigley, George Washington Hill, and Ogilvy; (2) there was no single 'first banner ad' — HotWired launched Oct 27, 1994 with roughly 6-12 ads live from 14 signed advertisers (AT&T among them), GNN sold a clickable web ad to a law firm in 1993, and Prodigy ran screen-bottom ads years earlier; the famous '44% CTR' attaches to the AT&T unit specifically and is self-reported.
gaps.why_it_matters: These are the two most-quoted 'facts' in ad history and the highest-probability targets for the adversarial-verification stage. Repeating them unhedged would undercut the project's calibrated-claims brand; both are still usable if graded as 'attributed/apocryphal'.
gaps.evidence: Quote Investigator, 'One-Half the Money I Spend for Advertising Is Wasted...', https://quoteinvestigator.com/2022/04/11/advertising/; Fast Company, 'The Trailblazing... History of the Online Banner Ad' (GNN 1993, Prodigy, no single first), https://www.fastcompany.com/3037484/the-trailblazing-candy-colored-history-of-the-online-banner-ad; Digiday oral history of the first banner ad (14 advertisers, simultaneous launch, 44% figure), https://digiday.com/media/history-of-the-banner-ad/.
gaps.recommendation: Add an 'attributed/apocryphal' grade to the claims.json schema (distinct from A/B/C evidence grades) and seed a myth-watchlist now: Wanamaker quote, first-banner-ad, '1938 radio overtook print', '1954 TV #1 medium', and any 'first ad agency' (Palmer 1841) superlatives.

gaps.title: The dot-com crash's causal role in creating the auction era is underweighted at the era 5/6 boundary
gaps.claim: 2001 was the demand shock that made the auction era: total US ad spend fell ~2.7% (~$7B), internet advertising fell 12% for 2001 (Q4 2001 $1.7B, -7.5% YoY) and broadcast TV fell 11.8-13.8% — collapsing the CPM banner/portal model and forcing Google off its original CPM-priced AdWords (2000) onto auction CPC (Feb 2002), while pay-for-performance search (Overture) kept growing through the crash. Newspaper classifieds also peaked in 2000, before the auction existed.
gaps.why_it_matters: The plan cuts eras at 2001/2002 correctly but treats the boundary as a product launch (AdWords Select) rather than a macro selection event. The crash is the evidence for the plan's own deeper thesis — accountable performance pricing survives downturns, impression pricing doesn't — and it is also the direct precedent for P3's question about ad-funded economics under stress.
gaps.evidence: IAB, 'Internet Advertising Revenue Totaled $1.7 Billion for Q4 2001' (FY2001 $7.2B, -12%; broadcast TV -11.8 to -13.8%), https://www.iab.com/news/internet-advertising-revenue-totaled-1-7-billion-q4-2001/; Venky Rao, 'US Advertising Revenue Trends and Their Link to Recessions' (2001: -2.7%), https://venkyrao.medium.com/us-advertising-revenue-trends-and-their-link-to-recessions-2000-2024-c28c1cf638fd; CJR (classifieds peak 2000), https://www.cjr.org/short_takes/craigslist_straw_man_1.php.
gaps.recommendation: Note in scope: era 5's EVENTS must include the 2001 crash as the mechanism-forcing event, and era 6's opening should frame the auction as the survivor of a pricing-model extinction, not merely a better invention. Also flag 2009 (the only down year for digital) as the stress-test replication.

gaps.title: Era 7's 'duopoly' baseline is already stale — retail media/Amazon breaks it, and 'one global figure' hides the China fork
gaps.claim: The duopoly framing is out of date for the P3 handoff: Amazon's ad revenue exceeds $60B in 2025 (worldwide ~$81B forecast for 2026), Amazon holds >75% of US retail media, and Alphabet+Meta+Amazon jointly took 53.6% of global ad spend EX-CHINA in 2024 — note that headline 'global' figures are published both ex-China and including China and differ enormously, so 'one global market-size figure per era' will silently embed that choice. Era 7 also omits the second antitrust outcome: the April 2025 ruling that Google illegally monopolized ad-tech (the programmatic stack), a different finding from the search-defaults case.
gaps.why_it_matters: P3 asks why ads aren't solving AI economics; the baseline it inherits must show that the newest fast-growing ad model (retail media) is closed-loop first-party-data commerce advertising — a structural mutation of the auction story, not a continuation of the duopoly. A stale 2015-era 'duopoly' baseline would start P3 from a wrong premise, and an unlabeled global figure will fail verification against whichever China treatment the checker picks.
gaps.evidence: eMarketer, 'Amazon's retail media ad revenues will pass $60 billion in 2025' and >75% of US retail media, https://www.emarketer.com/content/amazon-retail-media-ad-revenues-will-pass-60-billion-2025 and https://www.emarketer.com/content/faq-on-amazon-advertising--retail-media-dominance--prime-video-scale--agentic-ad-tools; Advanced Television (GroupM-derived: Alphabet+Amazon+Meta 53.6% of global ad spend excluding China, 2024), https://www.advanced-television.com/2025/05/21/forecast-amazon-2025-retail-media-ad-revenue-to-exceed-60bn/.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: era 7 must cover retail media as a distinct pricing/attention mechanism (closed-loop, first-party data, on-site auction) and the 2025 ad-tech monopolization ruling; require every 'global' figure in claims.json to carry an explicit ex-China/incl-China flag.

scouts.feasibility_notes: The seven-era structure, the auction simulator, and the readability-gated three-layer deliverable are all feasible as scoped. Three feasibility caveats from this lens. (1) The signature chart as specified ("a century-long ad-spend-by-medium dataset, 1919-2026") is not buildable as a single continuous series — Coen ends 2007, Magna backcasts only to 1980 on a different basis, and modern digital figures are net revenue while Coen figures are rate-card billings; it IS buildable as an explicitly spliced, seam-annotated chart, which is arguably a better artifact for a rigor-branded project. Overlap windows (1980-2007) exist for calibration, so the work is tractable. (2) The rigor bar (central estimate + 80% CI + grade + as-of date) is achievable from 1919 forward but not annually before 1919; a declared degraded mode for era 1 preserves the brand without fabrication. (3) The era-6 centerpiece is feasible and strong as mechanism pedagogy (worked numbers, GSP non-truthfulness), but the causal claim wrapped around it must be softened to survive the project's own adversarial stage — the DOJ record (defaults, TAC, pricing knobs) and the Overture history are public, well-documented, and directly contradict a pure 'better design won' thesis. That is a framing fix, not a research blocker. One bonus: Silk & Berndt note BLS PPI data for digital ad prices only begins in 2010, so any real-price (inflation-adjusted CPM/CPC) analysis before then is unsupported — keep the chart nominal or GDP-relative.
