gaps.title: The auction the centerpiece celebrates died inside the epilogue window, and the plan never records its death
gaps.claim: The quality-weighted second-price design that era 6 proves superior with worked numbers was abandoned or materially modified by Google itself during 2015-2019: Google Ad Manager moved all display/video inventory to a unified FIRST-price auction in 2019 (forced by header bidding), and the search auction was modified into RGSP (Randomized Generalized Second-Price) plus pricing knobs ('squashing', format pricing, launches Google internally described as raising prices ~10%+), as revealed in the DOJ search trial. The locked era-7 list (programmatic, duopoly, mobile, retail media) contains none of this, so the book's central mechanism story ends in 2008 as if GSP still runs the market.
gaps.why_it_matters: P3 inherits 'the auction design that monetized zero-price search' as its baseline mechanism. If P2 hands over GSP as the living mechanism, P3 reasons from a dead one: the 2026 market runs on first-price RTB on the open web and a revenue-tuned RGSP in search. It also completes the truthfulness nuance the plan already flags — GSP wasn't truthful, and under monopoly conditions Google tuned it as a pricing knob rather than a welfare mechanism. That is the single most important epilogue fact for P3's question about whether auction design or market power made search ads so profitable per query. The plan's own era-cutting rule ('cut where the pricing mechanism changed') implies 2019 is a mechanism boundary the current 7-era structure silently swallows.
gaps.evidence: Google's own announcement of the unified first-price move: 'An update on first price auctions for Google Ad Manager' (blog.google, https://blog.google/products/admanager/update-first-price-auctions-google-ad-manager/); AdExchanger on header bidding forcing the shift (https://www.adexchanger.com/the-sell-sider/googles-move-to-first-price-auctions-will-likely-put-a-dent-in-header-bidding/); Search Engine Land, 'What is RGSP? Google's Randomized Generalized Second-Price ad auctions explained' (https://searchengineland.com/google-rgsp-randomized-generalized-second-price-ad-auctions-explained-433053) and 'How Google harms search advertisers in 20 slides' — DOJ trial exhibits on squashing, format pricing, and RGSP as a 'pricing knob' worth ~10% revenue (https://searchengineland.com/doj-google-search-ad-price-manipulation-440207); Big Tech on Trial, 'A look inside Google's advertising auctions' (https://www.bigtechontrial.com/p/a-look-inside-googles-advertising)
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: era 7 PRICING must carry a three-beat sequence — header bidding (~2014-15) breaks the waterfall, unified first-price (2019) ends second-price on the open web, RGSP + pricing knobs (2017-2019, exposed 2023-24) end it in search. Era 6's centerpiece should end with a signpost ('this design wins — and watch what happens to it'). Consider one extra panel in the auction simulator: first-price with bid shading vs GSP, since the simulator otherwise teaches a mechanism the market no longer uses.

gaps.title: The per-query unit economics P3's whole question rests on is not in the 8-field schema
gaps.claim: P3's question is a per-unit comparison — ad revenue per query vs inference cost per query — but the schema's SCALE field only captures aggregates (total spend, % GDP, per-medium split). No field forces era 7 (or eras 5-6) to compute revenue-per-query, cost-per-serve, or gross margin per attention unit, so the epilogue as scoped hands P3 aggregates it cannot use and P3 must rebuild the unit economics from scratch.
gaps.why_it_matters: The reason ads 'solved' zero-price search is precisely that a search query cost ~0.2-1.1 cents to serve and returned ~1.6 cents to $0.05+ in ad revenue (estimates vary widely — which is itself why P2 should do this with its CI discipline). The reason ads may not solve AI inference is that an LLM answer initially cost multiples of that to serve, and SemiAnalysis-style analyses of 'the inference cost of search disruption' are exactly the calculation P3 needs, with 2023-2026 cost-decline curves (Pichai claims dramatic per-query cost declines in ~18 months). If P2's epilogue computes this once, calibrated and dated, P3 has its baseline; if not, P3's opening chapter is a research project P2 was better positioned to do.
gaps.evidence: SemiAnalysis, 'The Inference Cost of Search Disruption — Large Language Model Cost Analysis' (https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/the-inference-cost-of-search-disruption) — models LLM cost per query vs Google's ~1.06 cent cost / ~1.61 cent revenue per query; Kevin Kelly, 'How much does one search cost?' (https://kk.org/thetechnium/how-much-does-o/) — infrastructure-only ~0.3 cents per search; MediaPost, 'Google's Pichai Explains Cost Of Serving AI Search Queries' (https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/405924/googles-pichai-explains-cost-of-serving-ai-search.html) — per-query AI cost fell dramatically over ~18 months; revenue-per-search estimates ranging $0.08-0.50 depending on method and mix (Quora/analyst syntheses, e.g. https://www.quora.com/How-much-money-does-Google-Search-make-per-search) — the spread itself justifies the plan's 80% CI treatment
gaps.recommendation: Restructure slightly: add a ninth sub-line to SCALE (or a one-row 'UNIT ECONOMICS' extension used for eras 5-7 only): revenue per unit of attention (per query / per impression / per user-hour), cost to serve, and margin, each with CI + source grade + as-of date. For era 7, compute the search-ads trio (revenue/query, cost/query, margin) AND the 2023-2026 LLM inference cost-per-query series. This is the single highest-leverage handoff artifact for P3.

gaps.title: P3's premise has already been overtaken by 2025-2026 events the epilogue's locked list would drop entirely
gaps.claim: The locked era-7 list ends at retail media and contains no AI-x-advertising events, but by mid-2026 the P3 question ('why isn't advertising solving AI inference economics?') is being answered live: OpenAI began testing ads in ChatGPT on Jan 16, 2026 and rolled out broadly Feb 9, 2026 (Free and Go tiers, ad-free paid tiers); Meta began using Meta AI conversations to target ads across its apps on Dec 16, 2025; Perplexity launched ads (Nov 2024) then abandoned them by Feb 2026 for subscriptions after ads produced <0.1% of revenue; Google's AI Overviews (from May 2024) measurably cannibalize the click economics that funded the old model (Pew: 8% vs 15% CTR when an AI summary appears; only 1% of AI Overviews produce a click to a cited source; zero-click searches 56%→69% May 2024-May 2025).
gaps.why_it_matters: Without these events, P2 hands P3 a false premise: 'advertising is not (yet?) solving AI economics' reads as an open question when the record shows three divergent live experiments — OpenAI adopting the Netflix-style ad-tier hybrid, Meta fusing chatbot data into its existing ad machine, and Perplexity retreating to subscriptions because ad revenue per query could not compete. Perplexity is a natural experiment directly on P3's question and would be invisible in the current scope. The AI Overviews CTR data is equally load-bearing: it shows the incumbent's own AI is eroding the per-query economics P3 will treat as the baseline. P3 will have to restate its question as 'why did it take 3+ years, and does ad revenue per AI query cover inference cost?' — P2 must supply the dated state-of-play that makes that restatement possible.
gaps.evidence: OpenAI, 'Testing ads in ChatGPT' (https://openai.com/index/testing-ads-in-chatgpt/); ad-rollout coverage incl. Feb 2026 broad rollout (https://www.monks.com/articles/answer-engine-battles-navigating-chatgpt-ad-rollout, https://adventuremedia.ai/blog/chatgpt-ads-launch-2026-everything-us-businesses-need-to-know); Meta AI conversation-based ad targeting from Dec 16, 2025 (https://proton.me/blog/meta-ai-ads, https://www.dataslayer.ai/blog/meta-will-use-ai-conversations-to-personalize-ads); Perplexity's ad retreat — paused new advertisers Oct 2025, subscription-only by Feb 2026, ads <0.1% of revenue (https://www.moonsauceagency.com/blog/can-you-advertise-on-perplexity/, https://www.blog.udonis.co/advertising/perplexity-advertising); Pew Research Center, 'Do people click on links in Google AI summaries?' (https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/); Search Engine Land on the Pew study and Google's methodological dispute (https://searchengineland.com/google-ai-overviews-hurting-clicks-study-459434)
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: a final 2023-2026 beat in era 7's EVENTS (AI Overviews May 2024; Perplexity ads Nov 2024→retreat Feb 2026; Meta AI ad targeting Dec 2025; ChatGPT ads Jan-Feb 2026) plus an explicit dated 'state of play as of [freeze date]' handoff paragraph. Because this space moves monthly, give era 7 a declared data-freeze date so claims.json entries don't silently go stale before P3 starts.

gaps.title: Privacy shocks (ATT, GDPR, the cookie saga) are absent from the locked era-7 list
gaps.claim: The locked epilogue list has no privacy events, yet ATT (April 2021) alone cost Meta a self-reported ~$10B in 2022 revenue (third-party estimates $12.8B; ~75% opt-out rates), GDPR (2018) restructured European ad tech, and Google's third-party-cookie deprecation was announced (2020), delayed repeatedly, and finally cancelled (2024-25) — collectively the largest exogenous shock to targeting economics since the era began.
gaps.why_it_matters: For P3, privacy shocks explain WHERE ad money can go in the AI era: they broke third-party identity, which is why spend concentrated into logged-in first-party walled gardens and retail media. Any AI player hoping to fund inference with ads needs an identity/intent asset that survives the post-ATT regime — this is why Meta can fuse chatbot conversations into targeting and a standalone answer engine struggles. It also changed what TARGETING means (probabilistic modeling, on-platform signals, contextual resurgence — note OpenAI's ads are contextual, not behavioral). Omitting it leaves P3 unable to explain the 2026 concentration structure it inherits.
gaps.evidence: CNBC, 'Facebook says Apple iOS privacy change will result in $10 billion revenue hit this year' (https://www.cnbc.com/2022/02/02/facebook-says-apple-ios-privacy-change-will-cost-10-billion-this-year.html); Lotame $12.8B estimate and ~65-75% opt-out rates (https://www.cdpinstitute.org/news/apple-att-will-cost-meta-12-8-billion-in-revenue-in-2022-lotame-study/); Apple's own white paper on ATT and mobile advertising (https://www.apple.com/privacy/docs/Mobile_Advertising_and_the_Impact_of_Apples_App_Tracking_Transparency_Policy_April_2022.pdf)
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: a privacy-shock beat in era 7 (GDPR 2018, ATT 2021 with the $10B number, cookie-deprecation cancellation 2024-25) wired into the TARGETING field as the era's precision-REVERSAL — the only era in the whole arc where targeting precision went backward, which is a story point the schema's 'precision' axis should surface.

gaps.title: The antitrust endgame (2024-2026) is missing, and its remedies explicitly govern the AI era P3 studies
gaps.claim: The plan's epilogue has no antitrust beat, but within the era window Google was ruled an illegal monopolist twice — general search and search text ads (Judge Mehta, Aug 2024; remedies Sept 2025, final judgment Dec 2025) and open-web ad tech (Judge Brinkema, Apr 17, 2025; remedies pending into 2026, possible ad-server divestiture) — and Mehta's remedies explicitly extend default-contract prohibitions and data-sharing duties to generative-AI products.
gaps.why_it_matters: Two reasons P3 cannot skip this. First, the trials are the best A-grade evidence source the project has for era 6-7 mechanics — RGSP, pricing knobs, and take rates entered the public record through them. Second, the remedies are a boundary condition on P3's answer space: whether AI assistants can replicate the default-distribution playbook that made search ads a monopoly-scale business is now partly a matter of court order, and the search-ads pricing P3 treats as 'what a query is worth' was judicially found to be monopoly-inflated, not a competitive benchmark.
gaps.evidence: CNBC, 'Judge finalizes remedies in Google antitrust case' (Dec 5, 2025) (https://www.cnbc.com/2025/12/05/judge-finalize-remedies-in-google-antitrust-case.html); TechPolicy.Press on search remedies and their extension to GenAI (https://www.techpolicy.press/search-remedies-in-google-antitrust-case-can-work-even-if-company-stays-on-top/) and on the ad tech remedies phase (https://www.techpolicy.press/doj-vs-google-back-to-court-for-remedies-to-break-digital-ads-monopoly/); CRS summary of the remedies decision (https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/LSB/HTML/LSB11362.html); Digiday on the Brinkema ad tech trial closing stages (https://digiday.com/media-buying/everything-you-need-to-know-about-the-closing-stages-of-googles-ad-tech-antitrust-trial/)
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: 3-4 EVENTS entries (Aug 2024 liability, Apr 2025 ad tech liability, Sept-Dec 2025 remedies incl. the GenAI extension, Brinkema remedies status at freeze date), and mine the trial record as an A-grade source for era 6-7 PRICING numbers — it upgrades source grades the plan would otherwise fill with C-grade triangulation.

gaps.title: 'Duopoly' is the wrong 2026 endpoint — the epilogue's own headline concept is stale
gaps.claim: The locked plan names 'duopoly' as an era-7 pillar, but Google+Meta fell below 50% of US digital ad spend in 2022 and trend toward ~43%; the operative 2025-26 structure is a triopoly (Google+Meta+Amazon ≈ 72% of US digital), with Amazon (~$60B+ retail media revenue in 2025, >half of global retail media) closing on Meta, and TikTok/Microsoft/Walmart/Apple taking the rest; US retail media passed $62B in 2025 (global ~$140-184B depending on definition).
gaps.why_it_matters: P3's baseline question 'who has the ad demand, identity, and distribution to fund AI' gets a different answer under triopoly-plus-retail-media than under duopoly: the fastest-growing ad pool is commerce-intent inventory owned by retailers — the closest structural descendant of search's intent-based economics, and the pool AI shopping agents would either feed or bypass. Handing P3 'duopoly' hands it a 2017 map. Concentration numbers are also exactly the kind of headline claim the readability-gated prose will repeat, so getting the frame right matters more than usual.
gaps.evidence: eMarketer, 'As the duopoly stagnates, Amazon is hot on Meta's tail' (https://www.emarketer.com/content/duopoly-stagnates-amazon-hot-on-meta-s-tail); Marketing Charts, 'The US Digital Ad Market Is Looking More Like A Triopoly Than Duopoly' (https://www.marketingcharts.com/advertising-trends/spending-and-spenders-233301); PPC Land on triopoly share (~72%) (https://ppc.land/digital-advertising-triopoly-gains-overall-market-share-while-facing-competition/); eMarketer, 'Amazon's retail media ad revenues will pass $60 billion in 2025' (https://www.emarketer.com/content/amazon-retail-media-ad-revenues-will-pass-60-billion-2025) and '$10 billion in incremental ad spending will flow into US retail media in 2025' (https://www.emarketer.com/content/10-billion-incremental-ad-spending-will-flow-us-retail-media-2025)
gaps.recommendation: Restructure the era-7 framing: rename the pillar 'concentration' with a dated arc (duopoly peak ~2017 → sub-50% 2022 → triopoly ~72% 2025), and put the SELLERS field's 2026 snapshot in triopoly-plus-retail-media terms with shares + CIs. Note retail media explicitly as the intent-economics successor P3 will need.

gaps.title: The buyer side became algorithmic — by 2026 advertising is already AI-run, which reframes P3's question
gaps.claim: The epilogue's 'programmatic' pillar as scoped covers the sell-side plumbing but not the 2021-2026 demand-side shift: ~92% of US digital display now transacts programmatically (RTB ~62% of programmatic transactions), and black-box AI buying products (Google Performance Max, Meta Advantage+) absorbed a large share of budgets while independent incrementality testing (Haus) found 58% of brands got higher incremental ROI from manual campaigns and ~12pp over-reporting by the automated products — i.e., the machines that buy ads also grade their own homework.
gaps.why_it_matters: For P3 this collapses a false framing: the question is not 'will AI meet advertising' — advertising already IS an AI-vs-AI market where platform agents buy inventory from platform auctions using platform attribution. What made search ads profitable per query (human-legible intent, transparent-ish pricing) has been replaced by opaque optimization whose measured returns are contested. P3 needs this baseline to evaluate whether ad-funded AI would be an extension of this regime or a break from it, and the CREATORS field changes too (generative creative produced by the platforms themselves).
gaps.evidence: eMarketer, 'FAQ on AI media buying' (https://www.emarketer.com/content/faq-on-ai-media-buying--platform-tools--agency-strategy--how-win-2026) — incl. Haus incrementality findings (58% of brands, ~12pp over-reporting); eMarketer, 'FAQ on programmatic advertising' (https://www.emarketer.com/content/faq-on-programmatic-advertising--keeping-up-with-automated-ad-buying) — programmatic >$180B, ~92% of US digital display; RTB ~62% of programmatic transactions (https://sqmagazine.co.uk/programmatic-advertising-statistics/)
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: one beat in era 7 covering demand-side automation (PMax 2021, Advantage+ 2022, share-of-spend estimates, the measurement-conflict problem), touching CREATORS (generative creative), BUYERS (agencies disintermediated by platform AI), and PRICING (bid automation ends human-set bids).

gaps.title: The century-long ad/GDP constant broke after 2019, and the $1T-in-2025 headline is definitionally contested — both hit the signature chart's final segment
gaps.claim: Two data problems sit at the chart's right edge: (a) US ad spend tracked ~1.4-2% of GDP for a century but has grown faster than GDP every year since 2019 (when digital passed half of spend), breaking the constant the long series implies; (b) the epilogue's headline scale number disagrees across A/B sources — GroupM put global 2025 ad revenue at ~$1.08-1.1T (crossing $1T in 2025) while Magna put it at $979B (crossing in 2026) — a ~$100B definitional gap (media-owner revenue vs advertiser spend, what counts as 'advertising' once retail media and commerce fees blur in).
gaps.why_it_matters: P3's feasibility math depends on headroom: if advertising is a fixed ~2% of GDP, ad-funding AI inference means cannibalizing existing media; if the post-2019 break is real (ads absorbing commerce/trade-promotion budgets), there is new money. The epilogue must state which it is, with the definitional caveat — otherwise the signature chart's final years will silently mix incompatible series, and the 80% CI discipline will produce false precision. Bonus: the NBER paper and the galbithink 1919-2007 series are also the exact backbone sources the 1919-2026 dataset needs, so this is a two-for-one scoping note.
gaps.evidence: NBER Working Paper 28161, 'Aggregate Advertising Expenditure in the US Economy' (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf) — documents the ad/GDP ratio and its late-1990s shift ~1.4→1.9; galbithink, 'US Annual Advertising Spending Since 1919' (https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm) — the classic Coen-derived long series; eMarketer, 'Digital makes up over three-quarters of total ad spend in the US' (https://www.emarketer.com/content/digital-makes-up-over-three-quarters-total-ad-spend-us); Hollywood Reporter on GroupM's $1.1T 2025 forecast (https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/2024-global-advertising-forecast-groupm-trillion-2025-1235917863/); Marketing Dive on Magna's $979B 2025 / $1T-in-2026 forecast (https://www.marketingdive.com/news/magna-latest-to-downgrade-global-ad-spending-forecast-expects-979b/750871/)
gaps.recommendation: Collect data: extend the % of GDP series through 2026 and flag the post-2019 break as a named claim; for the era-7 global figure, present GroupM vs Magna as the CI bounds and state the definitional difference in the source-grade note rather than picking one silently.

gaps.title: The subscription-vs-ads hybrid (CTV ad tiers) is the era's business-model template for AI monetization, and it's not in the locked list
gaps.claim: The locked era-7 list omits CTV and the 2022-2024 streaming ad-tier wave (Netflix Nov 2022, Disney+ Dec 2022, Amazon Prime Video defaulting members into ads Jan 2024), which is the structural template every AI monetizer copied: free/cheap tier with ads, premium tier without — exactly OpenAI's Free/Go-with-ads vs Plus/Pro ad-free structure, and the model Perplexity tested and rejected.
gaps.why_it_matters: P3's question implicitly assumes 'ad-funded' and 'subscription' are alternatives; the 2020s record the epilogue should transmit is that the dominant model became the hybrid, and the choice variable is where the ad-free line is priced relative to per-user serving cost. TV's pricing arc (upfronts → programmatic CTV auctions) also closes a loop the book opens in era 3, which the compressed epilogue should at least gesture at.
gaps.evidence: eMarketer retail-media/CTV convergence and 2026 budget FAQ coverage (https://www.emarketer.com/content/faq-on-retail-media-networks-how-marketers-should-allocate-budgets-2026); the OpenAI tier structure showing the same hybrid (https://openai.com/index/testing-ads-in-chatgpt/); Perplexity's rejection of the ad side of the hybrid (https://www.moonsauceagency.com/blog/can-you-advertise-on-perplexity/). (CTV ad-tier launch dates are well-documented common record; a scoping-level cite pass should pull Netflix/Amazon launch coverage directly.)
gaps.recommendation: Note only (plus one EVENTS entry): a two-sentence beat naming the ad-tier wave as the era's model innovation and explicitly tagging it as the template AI firms adopted — cheap to add, high value to P3.

gaps.title: The signature chart's medium taxonomy breaks after ~2008 and the plan doesn't say how it will cut digital
gaps.claim: A 1919-2026 spend-by-medium series needs a post-2008 taxonomy decision the plan doesn't specify: 'digital' as one bucket makes the last 20 years — the part P3 uses — unreadable, while sub-splitting (search / social / retail media / CTV / open-web display) requires stitching sources with incompatible definitions (retail media double-counts with 'search' in some series; eMarketer, IAB/PwC, GroupM, and Magna cut the pie differently).
gaps.why_it_matters: P3 needs the digital sub-splits, not the digital total: its baseline is specifically search's share and retail media's rise. If the dataset ships with one 'digital/internet' column, P3 re-does the last two decades of the chart. Declaring the taxonomy now also protects the CI discipline — mixed-definition series produce spurious jumps that look like history.
gaps.evidence: galbithink long series shows the pre-digital taxonomy that must be extended (https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm); eMarketer's differing retail-media definitions across its own forecasts (https://www.emarketer.com/content/worldwide-retail-media-ad-spending-forecast-2024 vs https://www.emarketer.com/content/retail-media-ad-spending-forecast-trends-h2-2025); GroupM vs Magna scope differences (https://www.aaaa.org/research-report/groupm-global-ad-spend-forecast/, https://magnaglobal.com/global-ad-spending-is-poised-to-hit-1-trillion-inside-the-latest-forecasts/)
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: a one-page dataset spec fixing the medium taxonomy (with digital sub-splits from 1994 or 2008 onward), the primary source per segment, and a stated rule for the retail-media/search overlap.

scouts.feasibility_notes: The handoff is feasible without un-compressing era 7 into multiple chapters, but not with the locked four-pillar list (programmatic, duopoly, mobile, retail media) — that list is essentially a 2008-2019 story, and everything P3 needs happened 2019-2026 (first-price/RGSP, ATT, antitrust rulings, AI Overviews, ads-in-chatbots). Two cheap structural fixes cover it: (1) a fixed 'P3 handoff table' appendix to era 7 — a dated state-of-play snapshot with market size, concentration shares, per-query unit economics (search revenue/cost per query vs LLM inference cost per query), current auction regime, privacy/antitrust constraints, and AI-ads status as of a declared freeze date; (2) one added UNIT ECONOMICS line in the schema for eras 5-7. Two risks worth naming: the plan's own era-cutting rule ('cut where the pricing mechanism changed') is violated inside era 7 — 2019 (unified first-price + RGSP) is a genuine mechanism boundary, so either accept the inconsistency explicitly or mark 2019 as a sub-cut; and the 2025-2026 AI-ads material moves monthly, so era 7 needs a declared data-freeze date or its claims.json entries will be stale before P3 begins. Data availability is good throughout: the DOJ trial records upgrade era 6-7 pricing claims to A-grade, and eMarketer/GroupM/Magna/NBER/galbithink cover the quantitative fields. P3's framing itself needs one flag in the handoff: as of Feb 2026 ads ARE in ChatGPT and Meta AI, and Perplexity tried and abandoned them — so P3's question should be handed over restated as 'under what per-query economics does ad funding work for AI, and for whom,' not 'why isn't it happening.'

scouts.lens: Measurement and institutions historian — the infrastructure of audience counting (auditing, ratings, verification), the research industry and its conflicts, and the regulatory/self-regulatory layer, as determinants of who could set advertising prices in each era

gaps.title: MEASUREMENT is missing as a schema field, and it is the causal parent of both TARGETING and PRICING
gaps.claim: The 8-field schema cannot answer the project's own question — 'who set the price and why' — because every pricing regime in the plan's seven eras was created by a measurement regime, and the schema has no field for who counted the audience, how, and who paid the counter. Rate cards became enforceable only after the Audit Bureau of Circulations (1914) audited circulation; radio sponsorship was priced off Crossley/CAB then Hooper ratings; the upfront and the 30-second spot are priced off Nielsen; CPM presumes a counted M; the CPC auction presumes Google's own click logs. Targeting is downstream of measurement: PRIZM-style geodemographics (Claritas, mid-1970s) that enable Era 4's database marketing are census data plus ZIP codes, i.e., counting infrastructure.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without a measurement field the chapters will describe prices without the machinery that made those prices credible, and the Google chapter will misattribute to auction design what is partly a measurement-monopoly story. This is the difference between a story about ad formats and a story about market institutions — which is what the plan says it wants.
gaps.evidence: ABC founded 1914 by advertisers/agencies/publishers explicitly to combat false circulation claims that underpinned rate cards (History of Information, https://historyofinformation.com/detail.php?entryid=682; AAM, https://auditedmedia.com/about/who-we-are; JMU Circulating American Magazines, https://sites.lib.jmu.edu/circulating/about-this-project/about-the-abc-data/). Crossley/CAB 1930 advertiser-funded phone recall ratings, displaced by Hooper's coincidental method, then Nielsen's Audimeter (NYU radio ratings guide, https://guides.nyu.edu/radio/ratings; Jim Ramsburg, 'Radio's Rulers: Crossley, Hooper & Nielsen', http://www.jimramsburg.com/radiosrulerscrossleyhooperandnielsen.html; Beville, 'Audience Ratings', https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Ratings-Documents/Audience-Ratings-Beville-1988.pdf). Claritas/PRIZM built from digitized census + ZIP geography ('When the New Magic was New', IEEE Annals, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9927132/).
gaps.recommendation: Restructure: add a ninth schema field — MEASUREMENT (counting technology, counting institution, who paid it, known bias/crisis) — or rename TARGETING to 'MEASUREMENT & TARGETING' with measurement first. Cheap to fill: this literature is unusually well documented (Beville's book and worldradiohistory.com archives cover 1930-1988 nearly turnkey).

gaps.title: The signature 1919-2026 dataset has a hidden source seam at 2007 and no annual data before 1919
gaps.claim: There is no single continuous ad-spend-by-medium series covering 1919-2026. The only consistent series is Robert Coen's McCann-Erickson compilation, which runs 1919-2007 and stopped when Coen retired; everything after 2007 must be spliced from IAB/PwC, GroupM, Magna, or eMarketer, which define 'advertising' differently (treatment of direct mail, directories/Yellow Pages, classifieds, and now retail media varies). Before 1919 there are only benchmark-year estimates (Census of Manufactures 1865-1914; roughly $200M in 1880 to ~$3B early 1900s), so Era 1's SCALE field cannot be filled at the same annual rigor as later eras. Additionally, Coen's own pre-1940 figures were revised over time (1920s revised down ~15%).
gaps.why_it_matters: The signature chart is the project's centerpiece deliverable. An undeclared splice at 2007 or a silent definitional shift (e.g., retail media appearing as 'new spend') would corrupt the century-long visual and the claims.json layer — exactly the kind of error the 80% CI / source-grade rigor system is meant to prevent, but only if the seam is planned for.
gaps.evidence: Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset covers 1919-2007, compiled by Coen, digitized/augmented by Douglas Galbi, with explicit caveats on category drift and revisions (purple motes, https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/; Galbi, 'US Annual Advertising Spending Since 1919', https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm). Coen obituary confirms the series ended with his career (MediaPost, https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/292382/obit-ad-industry-forecaster-bob-coen-dead-at-93.html). NBER WP 28161 'Aggregate Advertising Expenditure in the US Economy' documents pre-1919 benchmark-only data and reconstruction issues (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w28161/w28161.pdf). Baruch College guide lists the fragmented modern sources (https://guides.newman.baruch.cuny.edu/c.php?g=188246&p=1243745).
gaps.recommendation: Collect data / restructure the deliverable spec: (a) adopt Coen/Galbi 1919-2007 as the spine and NBER WP 28161 as the reconciliation reference; (b) pre-register a splice methodology for 2007-2026 with a declared definitional bridge (and grade spliced years C, not B); (c) mark the seam visibly in the chart; (d) formally downgrade Era 1 SCALE to benchmark-year estimates with wide CIs rather than pretending annual coverage.

gaps.title: Era 1 is missing its institutional climax: circulation fraud and the 1914 Audit Bureau of Circulations
gaps.claim: The plan's Era 1 covers agencies, the 15% commission, and patent medicines, but omits that publishers routinely lied about circulation, making rate-card prices unverifiable until advertisers, agencies, and publishers jointly created the ABC in 1914 — the world's first third-party media audit and the template for every later measurement institution.
gaps.why_it_matters: The 15% commission story is incomplete without the audit story: agencies could only justify their role as buyers' agents once the thing being bought (circulation) was verifiable. ABC 1914 plus AAAA 1917 (the plan's own era endpoint) form one institutional moment — the market professionalizing itself — and ABC is the direct ancestor of the MRC fights that run through the Google era.
gaps.evidence: ABC founded 1914 in Chicago to combat false and misleading circulation claims; initially resented by publishers, then embraced as a guarantee (History of Information, https://historyofinformation.com/detail.php?entryid=682; Britannica, https://www.britannica.com/topic/Audit-Bureau-of-Circulation; AAM 'Who We Are', https://auditedmedia.com/about/who-we-are; Journalism History article on circulation as key metric, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00947679.2025.2508262).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: make ABC 1914 a named inflection in Era 1's EVENTS and the anchor of the measurement thread; frame Era 1 pricing as 'rate cards on unaudited claims' before 1914 vs 'audited circulation' after.

gaps.title: Eras 2-4 have no ratings-institution story, yet each era's pricing crises were measurement crises
gaps.claim: The plan names 'Nielsen demographics' as an Era 3 feature but skips the institutional sequence that repriced broadcasting three times: (a) Era 2 — advertiser-funded CAB (1930, Crossley recall surveys) overthrown by Hooper's coincidental method (CAB dissolved 1946), then by Nielsen's Audimeter, with shows cancelled and sponsorships repriced on methodology changes; (b) Era 3 — the 1963-64 Harris congressional hearings into ratings accuracy, which produced the Broadcast Rating Council (1964, now the Media Rating Council), the industry's standing audit body; (c) Era 4 — the 1987 People Meter switchover, which erased roughly 10%+ of measured prime-time audience overnight (children's dayparts down 20-50%), triggering make-good disputes and accelerating the cable/segmentation story the era is about.
gaps.why_it_matters: These are exactly the 'who set the price and why' inflections the schema's EVENTS field exists for. The People Meter episode in particular is the cleanest pre-digital demonstration that changing the counting method changes the market price — the precise mechanism the Era 6 centerpiece needs readers to already believe.
gaps.evidence: CAB/Hooper/Nielsen succession (NYU guide, https://guides.nyu.edu/radio/ratings; Ramsburg, http://www.jimramsburg.com/radiosrulerscrossleyhooperandnielsen.html). Harris Committee hearings March 1963-Sept 1964 led to industry-funded Broadcast Rating Council, later MRC (Media Rating Council, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_Rating_Council; HathiTrust record of the 1963 House hearings, https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/101710965). People Meter 1987: networks lost ~10% prime-time, CBS/ABC down 13%, Saturday-morning children's audience down 20-50% against ~$150M in ad revenue (CSMonitor 1988, https://www.csmonitor.com/1988/0106/fmeter.html; Headcount, https://www.headcountcoffee.com/blogs/media-history/1987-nielsen-people-meter-shifted-ratings-to-minute-data).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: one ratings-institution beat per era in EVENTS (CAB→Hooper in Era 2; Harris hearings/MRC founding in Era 3; People Meter 1987 in Era 4), written as repricing events, not media-history trivia.

gaps.title: The direct-response measurement lineage is missing, so the plan risks telling a false 'accountability arrived with the web' story
gaps.claim: Measurable, pay-for-performance advertising is a century older than the web: keyed coupons, mail-order response tracking, and split-run testing were codified by Claude Hopkins in Scientific Advertising (1923), and direct mail — a fully measured channel — was one of the largest line items in the Coen series throughout the century. Era 5's CPM-vs-CPC framing and Era 6's auction story are the industrialization of this existing direct-response logic (Overture and AdWords are keyed coupons at machine speed), not the invention of accountability.
gaps.why_it_matters: This changes the book's spine: the century is a two-track story (unmeasurable brand advertising priced on audience estimates vs measurable direct response priced on response), and Google's real coup was collapsing the two tracks — brand budgets flowing into a direct-response pricing machine. Era 4's 'database marketing' is currently the only nod to this track, framed as a niche rather than as the older, always-measured half of the market.
gaps.evidence: Hopkins 1923 is the first written description of split testing and coded-coupon tracking (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Advertising; scientificadvertising.com, https://www.scientificadvertising.com/authors/hopkins/). Direct mail is a distinct, large category in the Coen/Galbi series from 1935 on (purple motes, https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/).
gaps.recommendation: Restructure: introduce the brand-vs-direct-response distinction in Era 1 (mail order, keyed ads, Hopkins), carry it as a thread through Era 4 (direct mail, database marketing) into Eras 5-6, and state explicitly in Era 6 that Google merged the two tracks rather than inventing measurement.

gaps.title: The regulatory and self-regulatory layer is absent, and it repeatedly moved real money between media
gaps.claim: The plan has no thread for advertising law and category bans, yet these events changed BUYERS and MEDIUM shares in measurable, chartable ways: the muckraking-plus-Pure-Food-and-Drug-Act (1906) collapse of patent medicines removed Era 1's signature buyer category; the Printers' Ink model statute (1911) criminalized false advertising in most states; the FTC (1914) and Wheeler-Lea (1938) created federal deception jurisdiction; and the 1971 broadcast cigarette ban removed TV's largest single product category overnight — tobacco print spend jumped from $64.2M (1970) to $157.6M (1971) while total tobacco ad spend fell ~$80M, a visible kink in the by-medium dataset.
gaps.why_it_matters: The schema's BUYERS field ('who paid and why') will be wrong at two points — patent medicines circa 1906 and tobacco circa 1971 — if regulation isn't in scope, and the signature chart will show unexplained discontinuities. Self-regulation (NAB codes, NARB 1971) also explains why US advertising governance stayed private and industry-funded, which is the institutional pattern Google later exploits.
gaps.evidence: Printers' Ink statute 1911, widely adopted, strict liability (Hoofnagle, https://hoofnagle.berkeley.edu/2014/09/24/on-the-printers-ink-model-statute/; NBER WP 11927 on truth-in-advertising political economy, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w11927/w11927.pdf). Wheeler-Lea 1938 empowered FTC against consumer deception (EBSCO, https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/wheeler-lea-act-broadens-ftc-control-over-advertising; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeler%E2%80%93Lea_Act). 1971 ban and spend shift figures (EBSCO, https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/politics-and-government/cigarette-ads-are-banned-broadcast-media; EH.net 'Advertising Bans in the United States', https://eh.net/encyclopedia/nelson-adbans/; History.com, https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/april-1/nixon-signs-legislation-banning-cigarette-ads-on-tv-and-radio).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope as a light thread, not a field: one regulatory beat per era in EVENTS (1906/1911 in Era 1; 1938 in Era 2; 1971 ban in Era 3; children's-advertising and privacy beats later), each tied to a visible number in the dataset.

gaps.title: The 'what did Google change' answer is missing its institutional half: the seller became the auditor
gaps.claim: Era 6 explains Google's capture via auction design, but from 1914 (ABC) through 1964 (MRC) the market's rule was that audience counts come from a third party the buyer can audit; Google and the walled gardens reversed this — the same firm sells the inventory, runs the auction, counts the clicks/views, and attributes the conversions. The consequences are documented: Facebook overstated video view time for two years and paid a $40M settlement (2019); MRC accreditation became a rearguard action buyers demand from platforms; even Nielsen itself was stripped of MRC accreditation in 2021 after undercounting (a dispute worth $468M-$2.8B in national TV revenue by VAB's estimate), with buyers now attempting joint-industry-committee structures for streaming.
gaps.why_it_matters: This is the measurement lens's direct answer to the project's central question and the cleanest baseline for P3: any 'ads fund AI inference' model must specify who verifies the attention being sold, and the 2008-2026 record shows what happens when the seller self-certifies. Without it, Era 6 reads as 'better mousetrap' when it is equally 'auditor capture', and Era 7's programmatic fraud/viewability fights float without an institutional frame.
gaps.evidence: Facebook 2016 metrics errors, viewability as low as ~20% per agencies, $40M settlement, P&G/Pritchard pressure for MRC audits (MarTech, https://martech.org/facebook-measurement-update-metrics-viewability-verification/; Digiday, https://digiday.com/marketing/facebook-video-ad-viewability-rates-low-20-percent-agencies-say/; AdExchanger, https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/advertisers-forgive-facebook-measurement-blunders-mrc-audit-still-top-priority/). MRC viewability standards (Publift explainer, https://www.publift.com/blog/mrc-viewability). Nielsen stripped of national/local TV accreditation 2021, restored 2023; VAB $468M-$2.8B estimate (AdExchanger, https://www.adexchanger.com/tv-2/mrc-strips-nielsen-of-its-national-local-tv-accreditation/; PRWeek, https://www.prweek.com/article/1726281/nielsen-loses-mrc-accreditation-national-local-tv; Forbes, https://www.forbes.com/sites/derekbaine/2023/04/19/nielsen-trying-to-claw-back-ratings-credibility-gets-mrc-accreditation/).
gaps.recommendation: Restructure Era 6's thesis to twin claims — auction design (already planned) plus measurement vertical integration — and give Era 7's EVENTS the Facebook 2016 and Nielsen 2021 crises as the era's measurement beats feeding P3.

gaps.title: No conceptual spine for what is actually being sold: the audience commodity
gaps.claim: The plan lacks the one theoretical frame that unifies all seven eras: Dallas Smythe's audience-commodity argument (1977) that media firms' product is not content or ad space but measured audiences sold to advertisers — which makes measurement the factory that manufactures the commodity, and makes Google a manufacturer of a finer-grained commodity (intent) rather than a new kind of business.
gaps.why_it_matters: A seven-era history needs one sentence that survives every era transition. 'The product is the counted audience; each era is a new counting machine' is that sentence, and it comes with a citable academic lineage that strengthens the book's authority without adding jargon (compatible with the FK<=10 gate if paraphrased).
gaps.evidence: Smythe, 'Communications: Blindspot of Western Marxism', Canadian Journal of Political and Social Theory 1977 (CTheory, https://journals.uvic.ca/index.php/ctheory/article/view/13715); Dolber, 'Blindspots and Blurred Lines: Dallas Smythe, the Audience Commodity, and the Transformation of Labor in the Digital Age', Sociology Compass 2016, on its renewed applicability to digital platforms (https://compass.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/soc4.12387).
gaps.recommendation: Note only: adopt as the framing sentence of the introduction and the through-line each era's MEASUREMENT entry echoes; no schema change needed beyond gap #1.

gaps.title: Who pays the measurer is never asked
gaps.claim: The funding model of measurement bodies shifted across eras and biased the counts: CAB was advertiser-funded, Hooper and Nielsen were subscription businesses funded largely by the sellers being measured, ABC was tripartite, and the US has historically rejected the UK-style joint industry committee — until the 2020s JIC push for streaming. Seller-funded measurement structurally favors higher counts; buyer-funded favors lower; this asymmetry is part of why counts inflate until a crisis (1963 hearings, 1987 People Meter, 2016 Facebook, 2021 Nielsen).
gaps.why_it_matters: It converts the measurement thread from a list of organizations into a mechanism with predictive power — and it is the exact question P3 will need to ask about any attention-funded AI economics.
gaps.evidence: CAB advertiser-funded at 1930 founding vs Hooper/Nielsen commercial subscription model (NYU guide, https://guides.nyu.edu/radio/ratings; Ramsburg, http://www.jimramsburg.com/radiosrulerscrossleyhooperandnielsen.html); Harris hearings chose industry self-funding over regulation (MRC history, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_Rating_Council); current JIC/accreditation contest (Marketing Brew, https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2025/10/07/nielsen-measurement-accreditation-faces-uncertain-future-again).
gaps.recommendation: Note only: if gap #1's MEASUREMENT field is adopted, include 'who paid the counter' as one of its required sub-answers; no separate research track needed.

gaps.title: The 15% commission's death is untracked — the plan records its birth and then goes silent
gaps.claim: The commission system the plan introduces in Era 1 eroded through media-buying unbundling and fee-based compensation in the 1980s-90s and ended in scandal with the ANA/K2 media transparency report (2016) documenting pervasive undisclosed rebates to agencies — but no era in the plan owns this arc, so PRICING will silently switch models between eras without explanation.
gaps.why_it_matters: Agency compensation is the plan's own chosen entry point for 'who set prices' in Era 1; dropping the thread means the agency side of the market disappears just as Google disintermediates it — which is part of the Era 6 story (advertisers self-serve, no 15% to anyone).
gaps.evidence: ANA/K2 2016 findings: undisclosed cash rebates and rebate-like 'service agreements' pervasive in US media buying (ANA press release, https://www.ana.net/content/show/id/pr-2016-rebates-other; Marketing Dive, https://www.marketingdive.com/news/ana-releases-report-on-ad-industry-transparency-rebates/420535/; ANA initiative page, https://www.ana.net/content/show/id/industry-initiative-media-transparency).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope cheaply: one PRICING sub-line per era tracking agency compensation (commission → negotiated commission → fees/unbundling → rebate scandal → self-serve), landing the ANA/K2 beat in Era 7's EVENTS.

scouts.feasibility_notes: The plan as scoped is achievable, with two feasibility caveats from this lens. (1) The signature dataset's stated range (1919-2026) is honest only with a declared splice: the Coen/Galbi series ends in 2007, and the pre-1919 portion of Era 1 can never meet the same rigor — SCALE for 1840s-1918 should be pre-specified as benchmark-year estimates (Census of Manufactures 1865-1914) with grade-C, wide-CI numbers, or the plan will either overclaim or stall. (2) Adding a MEASUREMENT field is low-cost, not scope creep: the ratings literature is unusually well archived (Beville's 'Audience Ratings' 1988 and worldradiohistory.com hold most of Eras 2-4 turnkey; ABC/AAM and MRC histories cover the rest), so I estimate it adds roughly 10-15% research effort, concentrated in Eras 2-4 — which are currently the thinnest parts of the plan relative to the digital eras. The measurement thread also strengthens, rather than competes with, the Era 6 centerpiece: the People Meter 1987 episode gives readers a pre-digital proof that changing the count changes the price, which is the intuition the auction simulator needs them to arrive with. Finally, the thread lands exactly on P3's doorstep: 'who verifies the attention being sold, and who pays the verifier' is the institutional question an ads-fund-AI-inference model must answer, so the epilogue's measurement beats (Facebook 2016, Nielsen 2021, the JIC push) are the correct handoff baseline.

scouts.lens: Presentation scout — chart-form choice (data-to-viz verification), century-scale scrollytelling precedents, and auction-simulator / explorable-explanation precedents

gaps.title: Data-to-viz verified, but it solves only 1 of the 3 core design problems
gaps.claim: 'Data to Wiz' is data-to-viz.com (Yan Holtz and Conor Healy): an interactive decision tree keyed on DATASET SHAPE (numeric / categorical / time series / map / network), a caveat catalog of ~known chart pitfalls, and R/Python/D3/React code per chart type. Because its tree branches on data structure rather than message, interaction, or mechanism, it can route the century share-shift series (to stacked area / streamgraph / area small multiples) but offers nothing for the 8-field era-schema comparison (a qualitative fixed schema, not a dataset) and nothing for auction mechanics (no simulation or explorable content at all).
gaps.why_it_matters: If the design phase treats data-to-viz as the chart-choosing tool, two of the three hardest visual problems in the project fall outside its coverage and will be designed without guidance. Its highest real value here is the caveat catalog, which directly warns against the default form the signature chart would otherwise take.
gaps.evidence: Verified by direct fetch of https://www.data-to-viz.com/ — confirmed decision tree from data type, caveat gallery, and code examples in R/Python/D3/React. Complement exists: the FT Visual Vocabulary is keyed by FUNCTION (change-over-time, part-to-whole, ranking, magnitude...) which matches how this project actually thinks — https://github.com/Financial-Times/chart-doctor/tree/main/visual-vocabulary — with an interactive Tableau version by Andy Kriebel (https://datavizblog.com/2023/04/21/chart-literacy-financial-times-visual-vocabulary-andy-kriebel-and-tableau-part-3-of-a-series/).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: use data-to-viz as (a) the caveat gate every chosen chart must pass and (b) the starting shortlist for the time-series visuals; pair it with the FT Visual Vocabulary for message-driven choice. Explicitly note in the design plan that era-schema and auction visuals need precedents from data journalism and explorable explanations instead (gaps below).

gaps.title: The signature chart's default form (stacked area / streamgraph) is a documented readability trap
gaps.claim: A 107-year, 7+ medium share-shift series pushed through any chart chooser lands on stacked area or streamgraph, and both forms have well-documented failure modes for exactly this use: only the baseline series is accurately readable in a stacked area, and streamgraphs' shifting baseline makes mid-stack trends (e.g., radio's rise-and-fall, the exact story being told) hard or misleading to read.
gaps.why_it_matters: The century ad-spend-by-medium chart is named as the signature deliverable. If readers cannot accurately read when radio peaked or how fast newspapers collapsed from the hero chart, the project's central visual fails at its one job.
gaps.evidence: Data-to-viz's own caveat catalog covers stacking pitfalls (https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/stacking.html); Andy Kirk, 'Making sense of streamgraphs' documents the controversy around the NYT 'Ebb and Flow of Movies' streamgraph (https://visualisingdata.com/2010/08/making-sense-of-streamgraphs/); Streamgraph criticism summarized at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streamgraph.
gaps.recommendation: Restructure the deliverable: plan the signature chart as a SYSTEM, not one chart — a hero stacked/animated view for drama, plus per-medium small-multiple share lines (accurate reading), plus optionally a bump chart of medium RANK by era. Prototype at least two forms and test which supports the era-boundary claims. NYT 'How the Recession Reshaped the Economy, in 255 Charts' (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2014/06/05/upshot/how-the-recession-reshaped-the-economy-in-255-charts.html) is the proof that small multiples at scale carry a big economic story.

gaps.title: No cross-era comparative visual is planned for the 8-field schema (56 cells)
gaps.claim: The plan fixes an 8-field schema per era precisely so eras can be compared, but the deliverables list (prose chapters + signature chart + simulator) contains no visual that puts the 7 eras side by side on those 8 fields; 7 sequential chapters make comparison a memory task for the reader.
gaps.why_it_matters: The analytical payoff of the fixed schema — 'watch PRICING mutate from commission to rate card to upfront to CPM to auction' — is only visible if some view holds fields constant across eras. Without it, the schema does rigor work in claims.json but no presentation work.
gaps.evidence: Precedent for repeated-scaffold comparison: NYT's 255-charts piece uses a shared-scale small-multiple grid to make 255 industries comparable (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2014/06/05/upshot/how-the-recession-reshaped-the-economy-in-255-charts.html); The Pudding's visual-essay structure analysis shows recurring scaffolds are how they sustain comparison across a long scroll (https://www.storybench.org/pudding-structures-stories-visual-essays/). The Pudding's 'In pursuit of democracy' (https://pudding.cool/2025/11/democracy/) sustains one consistent dot-unit visual across 145 years — the object-constancy pattern that also matches the user's stated unit-viz preference.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: a repeating 'era dashboard' scaffold (same 8 slots, same positions, every chapter) plus one comparative matrix view (fields as rows, eras as columns) — likely the piece's second-most-shared visual. Design it in the same pass as the signature chart so the two share scales and color-by-medium encoding.

gaps.title: The auction simulator has no copyable template anywhere — highest-effort, least-precedented deliverable
gaps.claim: Searches found no interactive GSP/ad-auction explainer at any major outlet (NYT, Bloomberg, Vox, Wired, The Markup — nothing); the nearest precedents are Nicky Case-style explorables for OTHER mechanisms and paid classroom econ platforms. The plan specifies what the simulator must prove but not its pedagogical structure, and there is no existing design to adapt.
gaps.why_it_matters: This is the centerpiece. Explorable-explanation practice shows naive 'here's a sandbox' designs fail; the working pattern (Case's ballot and trust pieces) is guided constrained interactions per concept, sandbox last. Without that structure decided in planning, the simulator is an open-ended engineering risk. The absence of precedent is also the upside: a good GSP explorable would be the first of its kind.
gaps.evidence: Closest structural precedents: Nicky Case 'To Build a Better Ballot' — mechanism comparison via drag-the-voters simulation, open source, public domain (https://ncase.me/ballot/); 'The Evolution of Trust' — payoff-matrix game theory made playable (https://ncase.me/trust/); the Explorable Explanations hub (https://explorabl.es/, Data Stories ep. 103 https://datastori.es/103-explorable-explanations-with-nicky-case/). Classroom precedents proving students learn GSP-adjacent mechanics interactively: MobLab's Display Ad Auction game (https://www.moblab.com/edu/games/display-ad-auction, paid) and Veconlab/EconPort private-value auction experiments (https://en.wikiversity.org/wiki/Economic_Classroom_Experiments/Private_Value_Auctions). Numeric backbone for worked examples: Edelman, Ostrovsky & Schwarz, 'Internet Advertising and the Generalized Second-Price Auction' (https://web.stanford.edu/~ost/papers/gsp-final.pdf) — its small worked GSP examples, including the non-truthfulness demonstration, are the canonical numbers to animate.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope a simulator design spec BEFORE build: (1) guided sequence — pure bid (GoTo) → add quality weighting → add second-pricing → 'try to beat truthful bidding' step that lets the user overbid/underbid and see payoff (this is where GSP-not-truthful lands, borrowing Trust's payoff-reveal pattern); (2) sandbox last; (3) use EOS paper's worked numbers so the interactive and the prose prove the same arithmetic. Budget it as the largest single build item.

gaps.title: The rigor layer (80% CIs, source grades) has no on-chart representation plan
gaps.claim: Every number gets a CI and an A/B/C grade in claims.json, but no deliverable specifies how uncertainty and source quality appear IN the charts — meaning the signature chart will draw a crisp 1935 radio-spend line indistinguishable from a 2024 SEC-filing number, visually asserting false precision the text layer disclaims.
gaps.why_it_matters: The project's credibility promise is calibration. A chart that renders grade-C 1930s triangulations at the same visual confidence as grade-A filings quietly undoes that promise for every reader who looks at charts instead of footnotes — i.e., most of them.
gaps.evidence: Proven presentation techniques exist: Hypothetical Outcome Plots, used by NYT for jobs-report sampling noise ('How Not to Be Misled by the Jobs Report', Irwin & Quealy, 2014, https://www.nytimes.com/2014/05/02/upshot/how-not-to-be-misled-by-the-jobs-report.html; UW IDL explainer https://medium.com/@uwdata/hypothetical-outcome-plots-hops-help-users-separate-signal-from-noise-870d4e2b75d7). The user already validated a 'measurement jitter' pattern in P1's design — the same idiom extends here.
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: an uncertainty-encoding spec for the chart system — CI bands or HOP-style jitter driven directly from claims.json CIs, and a visual grade encoding (e.g., line texture/opacity by A/B/C) so data quality is legible on the chart itself. This also gives claims.json a second consumer, which will harden its schema.

gaps.title: The simulator's mechanic is a 2002-2008 vintage — Google's real auction has since changed, and the piece must say so visually
gaps.claim: An interactive presented as 'how Google's auction works' would be factually wrong for 2026: DOJ-trial evidence revealed Google runs randomized GSP (RGSP) variants, and Google moved display/AdSense to first-price in 2019-2021 — so the centerpiece simulates a mechanism that no longer runs as described.
gaps.why_it_matters: The simulator is the piece most likely to be shared out of context. Ad-tech-literate readers will flag 'Google doesn't do GSP anymore' and the correction will overshadow the (correct) historical point unless the interactive itself is date-stamped.
gaps.evidence: Search Engine Land, 'What is RGSP? Google's Randomized Generalized Second-Price ad auctions explained' (https://searchengineland.com/google-rgsp-randomized-generalized-second-price-ad-auctions-explained-433053); MonetizeMore on Google's second-to-first-price shift for display (https://www.monetizemore.com/blog/how-navigate-google-second-to-first-price-auctions/).
gaps.recommendation: Note only, plus one design element: title/frame the simulator as 'the 2002 auction' inside Era 6, and give Era 7 a one-line hand-off ('the auction itself kept mutating: first-price display in 2019, RGSP...') so the epilogue absorbs the correction preemptively.

gaps.title: No mobile/responsive plan for a scrollytelling piece with a sticky hero chart and a touch-driven simulator
gaps.claim: The plan commits to scrollytelling + an interactive simulator without addressing mobile, where the sticky-graphic pattern and multi-input auction controls degrade worst; The Pudding's published practice is mobile-FIRST design for exactly this reason, and majority readership will be on phones.
gaps.why_it_matters: Retrofitting a desktop-designed sticky-chart scroll onto mobile is the classic scrollytelling failure; the simulator's bid sliders/tables must be designed for touch from the start or Era 6's centerpiece is desktop-only.
gaps.evidence: The Pudding, 'Responsive scrollytelling best practices' (https://pudding.cool/process/responsive-scrollytelling/); 'An Introduction to Scrollama.js' — IntersectionObserver-based sticky-step pattern, the de facto standard implementation (https://pudding.cool/process/introducing-scrollama/, https://github.com/russellsamora/scrollama); 'How to implement scrollytelling with six different libraries' (https://pudding.cool/process/how-to-implement-scrollytelling/).
gaps.recommendation: Add to scope: mobile-first design constraint in the design phase; adopt scrollama (or equivalent) rather than hand-rolled scroll events; define a reduced-interaction mobile mode for the simulator (stepped taps instead of free sliders).

gaps.title: The visual spine (1919-2026) leaves Era 1 — 77 years of the story — off the signature chart
gaps.claim: The signature dataset starts in 1919 (matching the Coen/Galbi annual series), but the narrative starts in the 1840s, so the first chapter and half the timeline scroll along no data spine; the design phase has no stated treatment for the pre-1919 stretch.
gaps.why_it_matters: In a journey-first scrollytelling piece, the hero chart is the reader's map. If it appears only at chapter 2, Era 1 reads as prologue rather than as part of one continuous machine — undercutting the 'Birth of the Machine' framing.
gaps.evidence: Galbi's 'US Annual Advertising Spending Since 1919' confirms the annual series floor is 1919 (https://www.galbithink.org/ad-spending.htm); Galbi/purplemotes also compiles sparse pre-1919 estimates (Printers' Ink-era decennial figures) usable as point estimates (https://www.purplemotes.net/2008/09/14/us-advertising-expenditure-data/).
gaps.recommendation: Note for the design phase: render 1840s-1918 on the same timeline as sparse, wide-CI point estimates (visually distinct 'pre-instrument era' treatment — which also showcases the source-grade encoding from the uncertainty gap), rather than starting the axis at 1919.

scouts.feasibility_notes: Feasible from the presentation lens, with one skewed-effort warning. (1) Data-to-viz is real and exactly what the author likely remembered (decision tree + caveat catalog + code), but it is dataset-shaped, not message-shaped: it will serve the time-series visuals and act as a pitfall gate, and contributes nothing to the era-schema or auction visuals — pair it with the FT Visual Vocabulary. (2) Century-scale narrative precedents are abundant and directly reusable: The Pudding's 'In pursuit of democracy' (145 years, consistent dot-unit scaffold) is the single best primary reference and happens to match the user's documented object-constancy/unit-viz preference; NYT's 255-charts piece proves small-multiple grids for economic comparison; Bloomberg's 'What's Really Warming the World?' is the model for sequential candidate-explanation reveals (useful for 'why did Google win' rhetoric); the NYT Ebb-and-Flow streamgraph is the cautionary precedent. Scrollama plus The Pudding's process posts make the build path well-trodden. (3) The auction simulator is the outlier: no major outlet has ever shipped an interactive GSP explainer, so there is no template — the Nicky Case explorables (ballot, trust; both open source) supply the pedagogical pattern (guided constrained steps, payoff-reveal for the non-truthfulness moment, sandbox last) and the Edelman-Ostrovsky-Schwarz paper supplies canonical worked numbers, but this item should be budgeted as the largest build risk in the project, roughly equal to the entire rest of the web experience. Plan the chart system (hero + small multiples + uncertainty encoding driven from claims.json) as one design pass so encodings stay consistent across all seven eras.
